**Summary.** The paper experimentally demonstrates enhanced quantum parameter estimation sensitivity by employing a non-Hermitian observable readout technique on an optical interferometer. Using single photons in a Sagnac setup, the authors show that the resulting error variance is lower than the best Hermitian counterpart, even with noise present. This work provides a practical route for implementing and validating non-Hermitian concepts in quantum sensing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete experimental realization of using non-Hermitian physics in metrology. It is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics as it shows how engineered dissipation (non-Hermiticity) can enhance sensing while remaining physically consistent when measured fully.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to enhance quantum parameter estimation sensitivity beyond limits set by standard Hermitian measurements by utilizing non-Hermitian observables.

**Main result.** The experiment successfully demonstrated a reduced error-propagation variance using a non-Hermitian observable compared to the optimal Hermitian one, an advantage that persists under amplitude-damping noise.

**Method.** Quantum parameter estimation was performed experimentally using a single-photon Sagnac interferometer setup. The non-Hermitian expectation value was reconstructed by analyzing interference fringes from multiple output ports.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is a linear optical system utilizing single-photon probe states and a Sagnac interferometer. Non-Hermiticity is implemented through controllable, polarization-dependent photon loss within the measurement path.

**Key observables.** Error-propagation variance $(\Delta	heta)^2$, reconstructed complex expectation value of the non-Hermitian observable $\langle A' angle(	heta)$, and Classical Fisher Information (CFI).

**Important parameters / regimes.** State parameter $p$ (related to initial state preparation), noise strength $\gamma$ (amplitude damping), and the comparison between Hermitian vs. Non-Hermitian observables.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that while a non-Hermitian advantage is observed at the readout level, including all output ports in the full POVM measurement ensures consistency with standard quantum metrological limits.

**Figures summary.** Figures show interference patterns $I(\phi)$ for different observables and parameters, and plots illustrate the variance $(\Delta	heta)^2$ versus the state parameter $p$, comparing non-Hermitian vs. Hermitian performance.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the theoretical framework of using non-Hermitian Fisher information, describes the experimental setup involving SPDC and the Sagnac interferometer for readout, presents measurements showing variance reduction with non-Hermitian observables, and concludes by confirming consistency with standard quantum limits via POVM analysis.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The precision of quantum parameter estimation is traditionally constrained by the quantum Cramér-Rao bound, which is based on the Hermitian measurement framework. Recent studies of non-Hermitian systems have suggested new possibilities for enhancing parameter-estimation sensitivity. Here, we experimentally realize quantum parameter estimation using a non-Hermitian observable on a linear optical platform. The parameter is encoded in single-photon probe states and read out with a Sagnac interferometer, which allows us to reconstruct the complex expectation value of the implemented non-Hermitian observable from interference fringes. We observe a reduced error-propagation variance compared with the optimal Hermitian observable for the same probe-state model. This advantage remains visible under amplitude-damping noise. We further analyze the complete optical measurement as a physical positive-operator-valued measure (POVM) and show, through the corresponding classical Fisher information (CFI), that the observed non-Hermitian advantage is consistent with the standard quantum metrological limit when all output ports are included. Our results provide an experimental route to non-Hermitian observable readout and clarify its operational meaning in quantum sensing.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper develops the Floquet time-convolutionless master equation to model open quantum systems under periodic driving while retaining full memory effects. By applying this formalism to the spin-boson model, the authors show that non-Markovianity exhibits sharp peaks precisely when quasienergy degeneracies occur. This work offers a rigorous theoretical tool for understanding how coherent spectral features dictate dissipative dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, non-Markovian framework for analyzing driven quantum systems, directly linking spectral properties (quasienergy crossings) to memory effects in dissipation, which is crucial for understanding engineered quantum dynamics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is deriving a time-local quantum master equation that accurately describes the non-Markovian dynamics of open quantum systems subjected to external, periodic driving forces.

**Main result.** The authors derive the Floquet time-convolutionless (TCL) master equation, demonstrating it captures strong non-Markovian effects characterized by sharp peaks in non-Markovianity at quasienergy crossings.

**Method.** The methodology combines Floquet theory with the time-convolutionless projection operator technique to achieve a time-local description without resorting to the Markov approximation.

**Model / system.** The study uses an open quantum system model, exemplified by the driven spin-boson system (a two-level system coupled to a bath of harmonic oscillators). The dynamics are governed by periodically time-dependent Hamiltonians.

**Key observables.** Non-Markovianity measure (trace-distance based), quasienergies ($\epsilon_n$), and the evolution of the reduced density matrix components (Bloch vector $\mathbf{x}(t)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Driving frequency ($\omega$), coupling strength, bath spectral density parameters ($\alpha, \Lambda, eta$), and the driving amplitude.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation is perturbative, restricted to second order in the coupling strength. It also assumes an initial factorized state for the system-environment interaction.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate sharp peaks of non-Markovianity as a function of driving amplitude, linked to quasienergy crossings; they also show persistent trace distance revivals in the undriven case when $\epsilon=0$.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the general Floquet-TCL master equation. It then analyzes specific regimes (undriven, RWA circular driving) and focuses heavily on the degenerate quasienergy limit ($\epsilon=0$), providing explicit analytical forms for time evolution coefficients.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the dynamics of open quantum systems driven by an external time-periodic force. Combining Floquet theory and the time-convolutionless projection operator technique we derive a time-local quantum master equation which exactly takes into account the periodic driving, while treating the system-environment interaction within second order in the coupling strength without performing the Markov approximation. The resulting equation of motion for the reduced density matrix is called Floquet time-convolutionless master equation. Employing the example of the driven spin-boson system, we demonstrate that this master equation is capable of describing strong non-Markovian effects, while yielding the Floquet-Lindblad master equation in the Markovian limit. A characteristic feature of memory effects in such driven dissipative systems is the emergence of sharp peaks of the trace-distance based non-Markovianity measure as a function of the driving amplitude, which can be traced back to quasienergy crossings leading to almost decoherence-protected subspaces through a quasienergy-induced dissipative decoupling mechanism.

</details>

**Analysis basis:** full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
**Topic relevance:** 🔥 `non-equilibrium universality` **4/5** · `Keldysh / 2PI / non-Gaussian methods` **3/5** · `driven-dissipative phase transition` **3/5** · `methods for driven-dissipative` **2/5** · `non-equilibrium dynamics` **2/5** · `analog quantum simulation` **1/5** · `correlated / nonlocal dissipation` **1/5** · `correlated cavity matter` **1/5**

<sub>FIG. 1. RG flows for ˜u and wu at wD = 0 — There are two fixed points present in the system: the trivial Gaussian fixed point and the Model A fixed point. **Summary.** This paper uses field-theoretic Renormalization Group techniques to analyze critical dynamics in systems with non-reciprocal couplings between multiple order parameters. The authors find that, despite the system being inherently non-equilibrium, the critical behavior is robustly governed by the standard equilibrium Model A universality class. This suggests that non-reciprocity alone may not be sufficient to generate entirely new universal physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous theoretical tools (RG) to classify critical behavior in systems driven far from equilibrium. The finding that non-reciprocity does not change the universality class is a key result for understanding non-equilibrium phase transitions relevant to AMO physics and active matter.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether non-reciprocal interactions induce novel universality classes in critical dynamics, generalizing analyses from single to multiple vector order parameters.

**Main result.** The renormalization group analysis shows that the non-reciprocal couplings are RG-irrelevant, meaning the critical behavior is governed by the equilibrium Model A universality class despite the transition being into a non-equilibrium state.

**Method.** The primary method employed is field-theoretic Renormalization Group (RG) analysis, performed to lowest order in $\epsilon = 4 - d$, applied to Langevin equations describing the dynamics.

**Model / system.** The system models the ordering dynamics of two non-reciprocally coupled $n$-vector order parameters ($\phi_i \in \mathbb{R}^n$) governed by a noisy multi-component complex Ginzburg-Landau equation. This generalizes previous studies to higher symmetry ($U(n)$).

**Key observables.** Critical dynamics, scaling exponents ($\eta, \eta', \eta_c$), response function $\chi(k, \omega)$, and correlation function $C(k, \omega)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimensionality parameter $\epsilon = 4-d$, the number of components $n$, and dimensionless coupling ratios like $w_u$ and $w_D$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the structure of the Langevin equation is protected by symmetry, allowing for a perturbative RG treatment. The large-$n$ limit also simplifies calculations significantly.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates RG flows showing couplings flowing towards the stable Model A fixed point when $w_D=0$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the non-reciprocal coupled system via a Langevin equation, to performing an RG analysis by calculating Z-factors and solving Callan-Symanzik equations, culminating in determining scaling exponents at stable fixed points.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Non-reciprocal interactions find broad applicability in non-equilibrium and living systems. Their canonical implementation involves asymmetric couplings between two entities, which generally induce spatio-temporal patterns and time-dependent steady states that break time-translational invariance, representing a clear deviation from equilibrium physics. Although their phenomenology is well understood, whether non-reciprocal interactions induce new universality classes, and if so, under what conditions, remains an open question. In the present work, we perform a field-theoretic renormalization group (RG) analysis of the dynamics of two non-reciprocally coupled $n$-vector order parameters possessing a $U(n)$ symmetry, generalizing previous results to order parameters with multiple components, a feature that has been shown to generate novel non-equilibrium critical behavior in certain non-reciprocal systems. To lowest order in $ε= 4-d$, we find that the non-reciprocal coupling is RG-irrelevant, and the critical behavior is governed by the equilibrium fixed point of the Model A universality class of Hohenberg and Halperin with $2n$ vector components, even though the transition is into a non-equilibrium state. Our results demonstrate that non-reciprocity alone may not be sufficient to induce novel universality classes.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a sophisticated lattice model combining cell growth/degrowth dynamics with morphogen signaling gradients to simulate branching morphogenesis. By introducing local operators that enforce topological conservation, the authors study steady-state patterns. They find that these constrained steady states exhibit specific power-law scaling exponents ($eta \approx 0.67$), demonstrating how topology can regulate macroscopic pattern formation.

**Why it may be interesting.** The framework of using non-equilibrium statistical mechanics principles (like reaction-diffusion coupled with stochastic processes) to model complex biological pattern formation is highly relevant for understanding active matter systems and phase transitions in soft matter physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study focuses on controlling both the morphology (shape) and topology of branching patterns using a lattice model governed by morphogen concentration gradients.

**Main result.** The steady-state clusters formed under combined growth and degrowth, while maintaining topological constraints, exhibit a power-law scaling exponent for the radius of gyration ($eta \approx 0.67 - 0.68$), which is robust across different lattice symmetries.

**Method.** The research employs stochastic lattice models simulated via Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) and utilizes quasi-stationary approximations to solve coupled reaction-diffusion equations for morphogen fields.

**Model / system.** The system is a stochastic lattice model simulating branching morphogenesis, coupling cell occupation dynamics with the concentration of signaling molecules (morphogens). The dynamics include terms for growth ($
u^+$), degrowth ($
u^-$), and diffusion/reaction of morphogens ($c_r$).

**Key observables.** Radius of gyration scaling exponent ($eta$), correlation function $C(r)$, Euler characteristic ($\chi$), and steady-state cluster morphology.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Diffusion-limited aggregation (DLA) limit, Eden model limit, morphogen degradation rate ($k$), and the local topological control operator ($f_r$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is the quasistatic limit for the morphogen field, meaning its concentration relaxes much faster than the cluster growth/degrowth processes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate examples of morphogen-controlled cluster growth and potential sites for change. Comparisons are made between DLA, Eden limits, and steady-state dynamics, showing $R_g$ and $C(r)$ scaling behavior.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the coupled stochastic lattice model (growth/degrowth + morphogen diffusion). It analyzes limiting cases (DLA/Eden) and then introduces a local operator to enforce topological constraints ($\delta\chi=0$). The main results compare the resulting steady-state scaling exponents against unconstrained growth.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a lattice model for morphogen-controlled branching morphogenesis which combines ideas and concepts from non-equilibrium physics and developmental biology. In this model, the stochastic occupation dynamics of cells is coupled with signaling molecules (morphogens) produced by the cells. We investigate growth patterns governed by morphogen concentration gradients, spanning regimes ranging from the diffusion-limited aggregation limit to the stochastic surface growth (Eden model) limit. Moreover, we introduce control over topology by a local operator and study growth, degrowth, and steady-state dynamics of branched patterns. The topology-preserving steady-state clusters exhibit a power-law scaling of radius of gyration with cluster size, yielding the exponents $0.68\pm0.01$ in square lattice and $0.67\pm 0.01$ in hexagonal lattice.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces QuantumFCS.jl, an efficient Julia package designed to calculate Full-Counting Statistics (FCS) for open quantum systems. It allows researchers to analyze current fluctuations—like photon or heat currents—by computing high-order cumulants. The tool is demonstrated on complex models such as the Jaynes-Cummings system and circuit-QED engines, providing deep insights into non-classical noise phenomena.

**Why it may be interesting.** This is highly relevant as it provides a powerful, general computational tool for quantifying noise and non-Gaussian statistics in open quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding realistic quantum devices.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is characterizing current fluctuations (Full-Counting Statistics, FCS) in open quantum systems, moving beyond simple average currents.

**Main result.** The authors introduce QuantumFCS.jl, an efficient Julia package that successfully calculates high-order cumulants for various quantum transport and optics problems.

**Method.** The method relies on computing the cumulant generating function using a recursive algorithm applied to a counting-field-resolved density matrix governed by a tilted master equation.

**Model / system.** The framework applies to open quantum systems described by Lindblad master equations, demonstrated on models like the Jaynes-Cummings system and circuit-QED heat engines.

**Key observables.** Full-Counting Statistics (FCS), particle/electric/heat currents, and higher cumulants ($\langle\langle I^n angleangle$) revealing phenomena like antibunching and intermittency.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The calculation depends on defining monitored jump operators ($M$) and associated weights ($
u$). Benchmarks use specific parameters for heat engines and circuit-QED setups.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core theory assumes Markovian open-system dynamics governed by the Lindblad master equation.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 provides an overview of the FCS workflow, detailing the problem setup, the `LindbladFCS` structure, and inputs/outputs. Table 1 illustrates how different current types are defined via monitored jumps and weights.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the theoretical framework for FCS using a recursive cumulant algorithm, details the implementation in QuantumFCS.jl supporting sparse solvers, and validates it through benchmarks on photon counting (Jaynes-Cummings) and heat-current fluctuations (Circuit-QED).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Full-counting statistics (FCS) provides a systematic framework for characterising current fluctuations in quantum transport, quantum optics, and open quantum systems. We introduce QuantumFCS.jl, an open-source Julia package for efficient and flexible numerical FCS calculations. The package defines currents through monitored jump operators and weights, allowing particle, electric, and heat currents to be treated within the same workflow. It implements a recursive cumulant algorithm with dense, sparse, and iterative solver backends, making it suitable for models that are challenging for direct dense methods. We demonstrate the package on photon counting in a driven-dissipative Jaynes-Cummings system near the blockade-breakdown phase transition and on heat-current fluctuations in a non-linear circuit-QED heat engine. These examples show how higher cumulants reveal intermittency between bright and dim emission, antibunching, and provide probes of thermodynamic uncertainty relations. Benchmarks against an existing FCS implementation show substantial speed-ups.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops Liouvillian Counterdiabatic Driving (LCD) to eliminate the excess dissipation that plagues free energy estimation when rapidly driving stochastic systems. By utilizing the biorthogonal eigenbasis of the Fokker-Planck generator, they construct a correction term that forces the probability distribution to track instantaneous equilibrium perfectly. This provides an exact, computationally robust tool for non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous, spectral method for controlling non-equilibrium dynamics in classical stochastic systems, drawing strong analogies to quantum shortcuts-to-adiabaticity concepts relevant to open quantum system control.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Finite-time driving of stochastic systems causes excess dissipation, leading to a lag between the evolving probability distribution and the instantaneous equilibrium state, which degrades free energy estimators.

**Main result.** The authors introduce Liouvillian Counterdiabatic Driving (LCD), a framework that exactly cancels this non-adiabatic lag by using the biorthogonal decomposition of the Fokker-Planck generator.

**Method.** They construct the counterdiabatic correction operator directly from the spectral decomposition of the time-dependent Liouville operator, avoiding generalized coordinate transformations used in prior work.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by an overdamped particle governed by a time-dependent Fokker-Planck equation (Liouvillian $\hat{L}(t)$), verified using double-well and harmonic trap potentials.

**Key observables.** Non-adiabatic lag, excess dissipated work ($W_{diss}$), Total Variation Distance (TVD), and Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL divergence).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Driving speed ($	au$), spectral gap size, and the number of retained relaxation modes ($M$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on the exact spectral decomposition of the Liouville operator; numerical stability is challenged in deep metastability regimes where gaps close.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare diagonalization time scaling (dense vs. sparse/tridiagonal solvers) and show convergence metrics (TVD, DKL) demonstrating lag suppression across various protocols.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem of non-adiabatic dissipation in stochastic driving; it develops LCD using biorthogonal decomposition and gauge transforms; it validates this approach numerically on standard potentials while also analyzing computational scalability via sparse matrix techniques.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Finite-time driving of stochastic systems generates excess dissipation, causing the evolving probability distribution to lag behind the instantaneous equilibrium, and consequently degrading the convergence of nonequilibrium free energy estimators based on the Jarzynski equality. Escorted free energy simulations address the non-adiabatic lag by engineering control fields $\mathbf{u}$ that eliminate the lag, enforcing the trajectory-wise equality $\mathcal{W}_\mathbf{u} = Δ\mathcal{F}$, and yielding zero-variance estimators. However, constructing the escorting field in closed form remains a challenge, approached variously through flow-field methods, targeted free energy perturbation, or learned diffeomorphisms. In this work, we construct a complementary numerical framework based on gauge-type transforms instead of generalized coordinate transforms for perfect escorting based on the exact spectral decomposition of the time-dependent Fokker-Planck generator. The biorthogonal decomposition of the Liouville operator directly yields a counterdiabatic correction whose action on the instantaneous equilibrium distribution exactly cancels the non-adiabatic lag at arbitrary driving speed in formal analogy with shortcuts-to-adiabaticity techniques such as Berry's transitionless driving for quantum systems. Numerical verification for simulations of an overdamped particle in a time-varying double-well potential and harmonic traps confirms that the counterdiabatic condition is satisfied to machine precision, with the non-adiabatic lag suppressed by roughly twelve orders of magnitude in total variation distance and sixteen orders in KL divergence relative to the unescorted dynamics. As a diagnostic, we demonstrate vanishing dissipated work $\mathcal{W}_{\text{diss}}(t) \approx 0$ for the deterministically propagated Fokker-Planck density across all protocol speeds.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces the Bogoliubov-ratio framework to diagnose quantum information measures for any time-dependent two-mode bosonic system described by a quadratic Hamiltonian. By mapping the dynamics onto a single Riccati equation using the ratio $\lambda_k$, it allows researchers to calculate entanglement and purity metrics model-independently. This method is demonstrated in diverse physical settings, including cosmology and advanced optical parametric amplification.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, standardized diagnostic tool that cleanly separates the physics of the driving protocol (model-dependent) from universal quantum information metrics, which is highly valuable for analyzing complex open or time-varying bosonic systems in AMO/Optics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to create a unified, model-independent framework for diagnosing quantum information properties of time-dependent two-mode bosonic systems.

**Main result.** The state dynamics are entirely characterized by the Bogoliubov ratio $\lambda_k$, which allows for the direct calculation of various entanglement and purity measures without full density matrix reconstruction.

**Method.** The framework utilizes the Bogoliubov ratio $\lambda_k = eta_k/\alpha_k$ to reduce the complex state evolution governed by a quadratic Hamiltonian into a single, solvable Riccati differential equation.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by a general time-dependent two-mode bosonic Hamiltonian, applied successfully to both primordial cosmological perturbations and chirped-pulse nondegenerate optical parametric amplifiers.

**Key observables.** Reduced-state purity, linear entropy, Rényi-2 entropy, and von Neumann entropy, all derived from the squared magnitude $q_k = |\lambda_k|^2$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The time-dependent coefficients $\omega_k(\eta)$ (frequency/detuning) and $g_k(\eta)$ (coupling/squeezing strength) govern the evolution of $\lambda_k$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework assumes the system's dynamics can be mapped onto a normalized paired Bogoliubov representation, and it is valid for quadratic Hamiltonians.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes; however, the analysis involves solving differential equations (Riccati equation) to track $\lambda_k(\eta)$ over time ($\eta$ or $	au$).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the framework using a general Hamiltonian, derives the governing Riccati equation for $\lambda_k$, and then demonstrates its utility by applying it sequentially to two distinct physical examples: cosmology and optical parametric amplification.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a compact and unified framework for quantum-information diagnostics of time-dependent two-mode bosonic systems based on the Bogoliubov ratio $λ_k(η) \equiv β_k(η)/α_k(η)$. For a general time-dependent quadratic two-mode Hamiltonian, the state dynamics is exactly reduced to a single complex Riccati equation for $λ_k$. Upon tracing out one partner mode, the spectrum of the one-mode reduced density matrix is determined entirely by the squared magnitude $q_k(η) = \vert{}λ_k(η)\vert{}^2$. Consequently, we could construct the explicit, model-independent formula for the for the reduced-state purity, linear entropy, Rényi-2 entropy, and von Neumann entropy without reconstructing and diagonalizing the reduced density matrix on a model-by-model basis using coupled squeezing parameters ($r_k, φ_k$). We demonstrate the utility of this framework in two distinct non-stationary setups: primordial cosmological perturbations and a chirped-pulse nondegenerate optical parametric amplifier. In the cosmological context, our formulation clarifies how background-induced phase rotation and frequency softening regulate squeezing growth and state mixedness; in the optical domain, it captures the delayed onset, suppression of squeezing accumulation, and late-time entropy saturation induced by finite pump duration and frequency chirp. By cleanly factorizing model-dependent driving protocols from universal information-theoretic metrics, this framework offers an efficient, standardized diagnostic tool for a broad class of parametrically driven quadratic bosonic systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a comprehensive model to study how chirality affects the motion of an object (intruder) moving through a fluctuating bath. It successfully bridges two distinct physical regimes—the dilute gas limit and the dense hydrodynamic limit—by showing that the source of chiral transport changes fundamentally between these limits.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a detailed theoretical mapping between microscopic collision dynamics (Boltzmann) and macroscopic continuum fluid mechanics (Stokes/hydrodynamics), which is crucial for understanding non-equilibrium transport in complex media.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how chiral dynamics of an intruder are governed by its geometry when moving through a non-equilibrium bath, comparing results across dilute and dense hydrodynamic regimes.

**Main result.** The odd response (chirality) arises from distinct mechanisms in the dilute limit (fluctuation-driven) versus the dense limit (hydrodynamic edge currents), leading to a density-controlled crossover in dynamics.

**Method.** Theoretical derivation using Boltzmann-Lorentz equations, followed by approximations yielding Langevin descriptions, and comparison with molecular dynamics simulations.

**Model / system.** The system consists of an intruder of arbitrary shape immersed in a non-equilibrium bath of point particles. Chirality can be introduced via the bath, the intruder, or their coupling mechanisms.

**Key observables.** Odd diffusivity ($D_{odd}$), rotational damping ($\Gamma$), and the torque generated by chiral edge currents.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Bath density ($n_b$), restitution coefficient ($\alpha$), and the degree of chirality ($\Delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The Langevin equation is valid when bath-particle inertia is small compared to intruder inertia; in the dense limit, continuum approximations are used.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare parameters for different shapes (wheel vs. triangle) and illustrate how even/odd diffusivities change with bath density, showing deviations from dilute theory at finite density.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the collision rules, deriving the Langevin equation in the dilute limit via Boltzmann-Lorentz analysis, and then extending the framework to the dense hydrodynamic regime where edge currents dominate the torque generation.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We introduce and simulate an analytically tractable model for an intruder of arbitrary shape in a nonequilibrium bath, with chirality originating from the bath, the intruder, or their coupling. In the dilute regime, a Langevin description derived from a Boltzmann-Lorentz equation shows how intruder geometry governs ratchet effects and odd response. In the dense regime, the dynamics of the intruder are instead governed by the hydrodynamic modes of the bath and edge currents, which are described by a Stokes equation including a chiral torque density. Our results link shape to chiral transport and show that odd response arises from distinct mechanisms in the dilute and dense limits.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper applies Krylov complexity theory to analyze the dynamics of the BMN matrix model at large mass gaps. By calculating spectral properties and entropy, the authors confirm that the system exhibits quantum chaotic behavior while also characterizing low-frequency excitations as non-propagating relaxation modes rather than conventional quasi-particles.

**Why it may be interesting.** The use of complexity measures like Krylov entropy to diagnose quantum chaos in a highly interacting, strongly coupled system like the BMN model provides theoretical tools applicable to understanding thermalization and scrambling in complex many-body systems relevant to condensed matter physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To use Krylov complexity as a diagnostic tool for understanding quantum many-body dynamics within the BMN matrix model, particularly in the regime of a large mass gap.

**Main result.** The linear early-time growth of the Krylov entropy confirms the onset of quantum chaos in the BMN model. Furthermore, spectral analysis suggests that low-frequency collective modes are non-propagating diffusion or relaxation modes.

**Method.** The authors calculate physical entities like moments and return amplitudes by constructing a Krylov basis set for the system's Hamiltonian. They analyze the resulting spectral function and entropy growth over time.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on the BMN matrix model, which is a massive deformation of the BFSS matrix model relevant to quantum gravity and holographic correspondence. The dynamics are governed by matrices $X_r$ and $X_a$.

**Key observables.** Krylov complexity (spread and operator growth), moments ($M_n$), return amplitudes, spectral function, density of states, Krylov variance, and Krylov entropy.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Large mass gap ($\mu 	o \infty$) is the primary regime analyzed. The analysis also considers early time evolution ($t \sim 0$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The spectral function is treated as a distribution to handle divergences, and for spread complexity, the initial state is assumed separable.

**Figures summary.** Not specified by notes; the text describes calculations of moments, entropy growth curves, and spectral features near resonance.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically calculates observables (moments, return amplitude) using the Krylov basis construction. It then analyzes the spectral properties, diagnosing divergences as non-propagating modes, and finally computes the entropy to confirm chaotic behavior.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We use Krylov complexity as a typical diagnostic of quantum many body dynamics in the context of BMN matrix model at large mass gap. We calculate several physical entities, for example, the moments and return amplitudes at large mass deformation. We calculate them for both spread complexity of states as well as Krylov growth of operators in the matrix model. We propose a general expression for the moments at any given order $n$. We also discuss orthogonal polynomials for spread as well as operator Krylov complexity. In the context of the Krylov operator growth we further compute the spectral function and the density of states. A careful analysis of the spectral function near the resonance reveals various IR divergences in addition to the physical collective modes. These collective modes appear to be exceptionally stable due to large mass gap. On the other hand, the UV of the theory appears to be extremely damped due to higher scattering rates. We carefully diagnose these IR divergences near resonance which reveals that these collective modes are in fact non-propagating and should be thought of as diffusion modes or relaxation modes with infinite relaxation time. We also calculate the Krylov variance and Krylov entropy for the matrix model and in particular at early time. The linear early time growth of the Krylov entropy confirms the onset of quantum chaos in the matrix model at large mass gap.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors demonstrate that Machine Learning can effectively characterize quantum entanglement in two-qubit photon systems by analyzing raw coincidence count data from simulated measurements. By training ML models on these noisy vectors, they achieve high accuracy in distinguishing entangled states from separable ones without needing to reconstruct the full density matrix. This proposes a computationally efficient pathway for quantum state verification in experimental settings.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the practical challenge of characterizing fragile quantum resources like entanglement using noisy, realistic measurement data, which is crucial for experimental quantum optics and communication protocols.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work investigates using Machine Learning (ML) algorithms to identify and quantify quantum entanglement directly from noisy measurement statistics, bypassing complex density matrix reconstruction.

**Main result.** ML methods achieve very high classification accuracy for distinguishing separable from entangled states, suggesting an efficient alternative to conventional state analysis under simulated noise conditions.

**Method.** Supervised ML algorithms (e.g., Random Forests, SVMs) are trained on 16-dimensional measurement vectors derived from simulated SIC-POVM measurements of polarization-entangled photon pairs.

**Model / system.** The system involves two-qubit polarization states analyzed using simulated symmetric, informationally complete POVM (SIC-POVM) measurement data. The analysis focuses on Werner states and Bell states to cover the entanglement spectrum.

**Key observables.** Classification of separable vs. entangled states; continuous estimation of Concurrence ($C(ho)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Poissonian shot noise level (related to total photon count $N$); entanglement parameter $p$ for Werner states.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is limited to simulated data affected by Poissonian counting noise, and the performance relies on the representativeness of the training set.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically applies various ML techniques (classification/regression) to datasets representing known entangled and separable states derived from simulating quantum measurements.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we investigate the application of Machine Learning (ML) algorithms to the identification and quantitative characterization of quantum entanglement in polarization-entangled photon pairs. The analysis is based on simulated symmetric, informationally complete, positive operator-valued measure (SIC-POVM) measurement data, where each two-qubit state is represented by a 16-dimensional measurement vector corresponding to experimentally accessible coincidence counts. The generated SIC-POVM measurement data include Poissonian shot noise. Several supervised ML algorithms, including Logistic Regression, k-Nearest Neighbors, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines, and Random Forests, are applied to the classification of separable and entangled states directly from raw measurement data, without explicit density matrix reconstruction or the use of conventional separability criteria. The study additionally explores clustering methods and nonlinear regression techniques for estimating continuous entanglement measures. The obtained results demonstrate that ML methods can achieve very high classification accuracy, even under extremely limited training conditions. These findings indicate that ML may provide an efficient alternative to conventional quantum-state analysis under simulated Poissonian noise conditions.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes an interacting p-wave magnet wire on a ring, showing that the magnetic texture winding imposes a global boundary condition. This topology dictates a switch in fermion parity between neighboring states, providing a robust, number-conserving probe of topological pairing mechanisms.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete realization where geometric/topological constraints (magnetic texture) dictate global many-body properties (fermion parity), which is highly relevant for understanding topological superconductivity in engineered materials or superconducting circuits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how the winding number of a magnetic texture controls fundamental fermion-parity switches within an interacting p-wave magnet wire geometry.

**Main result.** A global parity constraint causes neighboring phase-winding branches to reverse their fermion-parity assignment when the winding changes by one, demonstrating that the boundary condition is controlled by topology rather than local band structure.

**Method.** The research employs a combination of exact fixed-number derivations and advanced numerical techniques like Density-Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) simulations.

**Model / system.** The system is an interacting p-wave magnet wire realized on a ring geometry, modeled by Hamiltonians incorporating hopping, attraction, and exchange coupling modulated by local spin textures.

**Key observables.** Signed parity splitting ($D_p(M)$), central charge ($c$) extracted from entanglement entropy, and finite-size curvatures ($ho_s$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The winding number ($M$), the ring circumference ($L$), and the interaction strength parameters ($U, J$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a fixed particle number sector and that the system can be mapped to low-energy theories involving charge and neutral Majorana modes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate pitch changes and parity sign reversals across adjacent textures; other figures show scaling behavior of energy splittings and entanglement entropy supporting critical transitions.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the exact boundary condition imposed by magnetic winding to using DMRG simulations to observe parity reversal, followed by low-energy continuum analysis to characterize the nature of the quantum phase transition via central charge calculations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Coplanar magnetic spirals map locally onto uniform spin--orbit-coupled wires, but on a ring the rotating spin frame can change the electronic boundary condition. We prove, level by level in every fixed-particle-number sector, that even and odd texture windings impose boundary phases separated by half the single-electron flux period. Changing the winding by one also changes the physical pitch in inverse proportion to the circumference; a symmetric comparison removes this leading pitch correction. In the number-conserving topological phase, a global parity constraint then reverses the fermion-parity assignment of neighboring phase-winding branches. Density-matrix renormalization-group simulations show this reversal, support an Ising transition coexisting with a gapless charge mode, and relate the finite-size parity splitting to an independently calculated charge stiffness. Magnetic-texture winding thus changes the many-body spectrum through a global boundary condition that is not determined by the local band dispersion, providing a closed-geometry, number-conserving probe of topological pairing.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a scalable tomography protocol for fermionic many-body states by exploiting particle permutation symmetry. It shows that the full state information can be captured using only the total particle number distribution and the occupation of one collective mode, both measurable in cold atom setups. This opens a pathway to characterize strongly correlated quantum matter experimentally.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides an information-theoretic characterization tool that translates difficult quantum state reconstruction problems into measurable observables ($p_q, 
u_q$) directly accessible in modern ultracold atom experiments.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a scalable quantum state tomography protocol for fermionic many-body states that avoids the exponential measurement cost associated with full reconstruction.

**Main result.** The permutation-symmetrized density matrix can be fully reconstructed using only two quantities—the total particle number distribution ($p_q$) and the conditional occupation of a single collective mode ($
u_q$)—which scale linearly with system size.

**Method.** The protocol leverages $U(1)$ particle-number symmetry to decompose the state and utilizes properties derived from permutation invariance (Schur's Lemma) to simplify the required observables.

**Model / system.** The theory is applied to fermionic many-body states, particularly those with $U(1)$ particle-number symmetry, demonstrated using models like the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model and free-fermion chains in optical lattices.

**Key observables.** Total particle-number distribution ($p_q$) and conditional occupation of a uniform mode ($
u_q$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** System size ($N$), temperature/inverse coupling strength ($eta$), and the filling parameter ($\varrho$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The protocol is restricted to states with $U(1)$ particle-number symmetry, and some derivations rely on asymptotic approximations (e.g., Stirling's formula).

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 shows reconstruction using the SYK model via estimated $
u_q$ and $p_q$. Figure 2 demonstrates calculating von Neumann entropy for free fermions across a Lifshitz transition, showing predicted nonanalyticity.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the scalability problem of tomography, derives the PIQT protocol based on symmetry constraints, applies it to reconstruct complex states (SYK), and then uses the framework to calculate thermodynamic quantities like von Neumann entropy for free fermions near a critical point.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum state tomography provides complete information about a quantum state, but its measurement cost generally grows exponentially with system size. In many-particle quantum simulators, this challenge is further compounded by the limited accessibility of local measurements and controls. Here we develop a tomography protocol for permutation-invariant fermionic many-body states with U(1) particle-number symmetry. We show that any such state is completely determined by the distribution of the total particle number and the occupation of a single collective mode within each particle-number sector, both of which are accessible in current ultracold-atom experiments. The number of required observables scales only linearly with the system size. More generally, the protocol reconstructs the permutation-symmetrized component of arbitrary U(1)-symmetric fermionic states, which can still encode nontrivial many-body and state-level structure beyond conventional few-body observables. We demonstrate this protocol in interacting non-Gaussian states of the complex Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and in free-fermion chains across a Lifshitz transition. This framework opens a route toward information-theoretic characterization of strongly correlated itinerant quantum matter in experimentally realistic fermionic quantum simulators.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper details a novel technique to certify and quantify spatial entanglement in photon pairs generated by SPDC. By employing stimulated parametric down conversion (StimPDC), the authors replace slow coincidence counting with simple intensity measurements on the idler beam. This method successfully verifies entanglement using established witnesses, proving its utility for quantum optics experiments where precise photon detection is challenging.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly practical experimental protocol for quantum optics that bypasses major technical hurdles in quantum measurement, making entanglement characterization accessible under difficult experimental conditions.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is certifying and quantifying spatial entanglement of photon pairs generated by SPDC without relying on slow, coincidence-counting measurements.

**Main result.** Spatial entanglement and EPR steering can be robustly certified using only intensity measurements from the idler beam via stimulated parametric down conversion (StimPDC).

**Method.** The authors use StimPDC by seeding the signal mode with a bright classical beam, allowing them to measure conditional idler states using standard intensity detectors instead of coincidence counting.

**Model / system.** The system involves entangled photon pairs generated via SPDC. The measurement technique utilizes stimulated emission into the idler field, which is then analyzed in both transverse position and momentum bases.

**Key observables.** Entanglement witnesses (Reid criterion, MGVT product) and the Fedorov ratio ($R$), calculated from measured conditional variances ($\sigma^2$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The correlation strength is tracked by varying the pump waist size; finite seed widths only broaden measured variances.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes paraxial and quasi-monochromatic approximations, and the method's robustness relies on imperfections only broadening measurements, preventing false positives.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate conceptual diagrams for position-space and momentum-space seeding (Fig. 1). Other figures show measured near-field/far-field intensity profiles and correlation plots confirming expected linear fits.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the StimPDC method to replace coincidence counting, derives the conditional idler state, applies entanglement witnesses (Reid, MGVT), calculates the Fedorov ratio, and presents results demonstrating robust certification of spatial entanglement using only intensity measurements.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Using stimulated emission, a photon pair source can be characterized by seeding the signal mode with a bright classical beam and measuring the stimulated idler field, thus replacing two-photon coincidence counting with classical intensity detection. We apply this approach to the continuous transverse spatial degrees of freedom of a down conversion source and show that it is possible to certify spatial entanglement with only intensity measurements. We demonstrate this capability through variance-based entanglement and steering witnesses, as well as the Fedorov ratio. This method is useful for studying entanglement properties of photon pair sources in conditions where alignment and photon counting measurements are difficult and time-consuming.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a comprehensive, fully vectorial theory to analyze how position measurements are limited by photon scattering noise in levitated nanoparticles. By using the Angular Spectrum Representation, it accurately models non-paraxial effects, demonstrating that structured light like radial polarization can suppress unwanted axial backaction forces compared to standard Gaussian traps.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides advanced theoretical tools for designing next-generation quantum sensors by rigorously accounting for the polarization and angular structure of light fields on measurement backaction limits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a fully vectorial, semiclassical formalism for characterizing position measurement backaction noise and detection efficiency in optically levitated dipolar scatterers.

**Main result.** The vectorial approach shows that structured light fields, such as radially polarized beams, can fundamentally suppress axial measurement backaction compared to conventional Gaussian traps.

**Method.** The authors use the angular spectrum representation (ASR) within a semiclassical scattering formalism to calculate momentum transfer and detection efficiency, moving beyond paraxial approximations.

**Model / system.** The system involves levitating mesoscopic nanoparticles trapped by arbitrary optical fields. The theoretical model incorporates Langevin dynamics and treats the measurement process using photon shot noise statistics.

**Key observables.** Information radiation pattern, mode-matching efficiency ($\eta_{det,q}$), backaction force spectral density ($S_{b,k,q}$), and the resulting effective imprecision noise ($\Delta x_{	ext{eff}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The generalized geometric factor ($	ext{C}_q$), filling factor ($f_0$), and the comparison between linearly vs. radially polarized beams.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the Rayleigh scattering regime ($a \ll \lambda$) and employs a semiclassical treatment for the trapping field, while using ASR to handle non-paraxial effects.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare optomechanical parameters (like backaction rates) for different polarizations as a function of beam filling factor, highlighting differences between vectorial and paraxial approximations.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from developing the general vectorial scattering formalism using ASR to calculate momentum transfer ($	ext{C}_q$), then applies this framework to quantify detection efficiency ($\eta_{det,q}$), culminating in specific examples comparing Gaussian versus radially polarized traps.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a fully vectorial, semiclassical scattering formalism for optically levitated dipolar scatterers, expressed within the angular spectrum representation and applicable to arbitrary trapping-field configurations as well as to high--numerical-aperture focusing. Within this framework, we introduce the information radiation pattern to characterize the angular distribution of position-dependent information and use a Richards--Wolf projection of the scattered field onto the local-oscillator mode to quantify the resulting mode-matching efficiency, yielding experimentally realistic forward- and backward-detection efficiencies. As a worked example, we apply the formalism to a radially polarized trapping beam and confirm that the axial recoil heating rate is reduced relative to a conventional linearly polarized Gaussian tweezer. The theoretical framework is implemented in LevitationToolbox, an open-source Python package intended to support the design and optimization of near-Heisenberg-limited levitated optomechanical experiments.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes using current cross-correlations as a superior diagnostic tool to verify the existence of Poor Man's Majorana modes in quantum dot arrays. By analyzing how these correlations behave when tuning away from ideal sweet spots, the authors demonstrate that only true topological states exhibit characteristic robustness. This provides a clear experimental pathway for confirming non-local entanglement signatures.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, measurable signature (noise correlation) that can distinguish between trivial and topological zero-energy states, which is crucial for experimental realization of Majorana physics in superconducting nanostructures.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The authors aim to develop diagnostic methods beyond standard differential conductance spectroscopy to verify the true non-locality and topological order of Poor Man's Majorana (PMM) modes.

**Main result.** Current cross-correlations are shown to be robust, exhibiting remarkable stability around the PMM sweet spot with respect to outer dot detuning, which distinguishes true topologically protected PMMs from false ones.

**Method.** The study employs advanced transport theory, calculating zero-frequency current cross-correlation functions ($S_{LR}$) using the Keldysh Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) formalism and scattering matrix techniques.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by a minimal Kitaev chain (MKC) setup with three quantum dots, emulating a topological superconductor. The physics is described using the Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian in Nambu spinor space.

**Key observables.** Current cross-correlations ($S_{LR}$), local conductance ($G_{LL}$), and the Fano factor ($F_{LL}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis focuses on the PMM sweet spot, zero energy ($E=0$), and varying detuning ($\delta$) of outer quantum dots.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations assume the $T=0$ limit for simplicity in Fermi functions and utilize the wide-band limit approximation for self-energies from normal leads.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the MKC device schematic, comparing true vs. false PMM modes under detuning; they also show energy landscapes around sweet spots and calculated local/nonlocal current correlation signatures ($S_{LL}$ and $S_{LR}$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the limitations of conductance spectroscopy to deriving the theoretical framework for current cross-correlations using NEGF, culminating in demonstrating the unique diagnostic power of these correlations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The minimal Kitaev chain that emulates a topological superconductor with three quantum dots offers a tunable platform for potentially hosting poor man's Majorana (PMM) modes. Asserting the need to go beyond differential conductance spectroscopy, we introduce current-current correlations as a viable framework for verifying their true non-locality. The robustness of the PMM modes, specifically with respect to delocalization as the system is tuned away from sweet spots, we show, is embedded in the relative magnitudes of the nonlocal transport processes. This aspect is adeptly captured by current cross-correlations, whose features show remarkable stability around the PMM sweet spot, specifically with respect to the detuning of an outer dot. We establish this as a prominent feature and a diagnostic for true PMMs even in the short chain limit. Our results accentuate the need for current cross-correlation measurements as a diagnostic framework for unambiguously verifying true non-locality of entangled states as well as topologically protected states.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper addresses laser phase noise, a major hurdle for trapped-ion qubits, by implementing an active Pound-Drever-Hall feedforward stabilization system. This technique successfully suppresses detrimental servo-bump phase noise near the operating frequency. The results confirm that this stabilization significantly improves qubit coherence time and gate fidelity across previously restricted operational regimes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides an essential experimental blueprint for mitigating technical noise sources (laser phase noise) that fundamentally limit the achievable gate fidelity in trapped-ion quantum computing architectures.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Laser phase noise is a critical limiting factor for achieving high gate fidelities and coherence times in trapped-ion quantum systems.

**Main result.** The implementation of Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) feedforward stabilization successfully suppresses servo-bump phase noise by 15 dB, allowing optical qubit operations to maintain coherence even when the Rabi frequency is near this problematic noise region.

**Method.** The authors employed an active phase-noise stabilization system using a fiber electro-optic modulator (EOM) and electrical feedforward servo, validated through Delayed Self-Heterodyne Interferometry (DSHI).

**Model / system.** The experiment uses a trapped-ion optical qubit platform based on Barium ions ($	ext{Ba}^+$) at 1762 nm. The analysis models the qubit dynamics using Pauli-transfer matrices and stochastic differential equations to track coherence decay.

**Key observables.** Coherence time ($T_2$), gate fidelity ($\epsilon_{	ext{avg}}$), Rabi oscillation amplitude decay, and measured phase noise suppression (15 dB).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Rabi frequency relative to the servo-bump bandwidth; stabilization level of 15 dB; operating wavelength of 1762 nm.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The technique's applicability was experimentally verified for optical qubits, and coherence time analysis relies on fitting $\log_{10} T_2$ vs. $\Delta 	ext{dB}$.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup involving PDH stabilization and DSHI measurement, comparing noise suppression results with linewidth measurements.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying laser phase noise as a limitation to detailing the PDH feedforward technique, measuring its performance via DSHI, and finally demonstrating the resulting improvement in qubit coherence time through Rabi oscillation analysis.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Laser phase noise is one of the limiting factors that dictate gate fidelities and coherence times in trapped-ion quantum systems. Previous studies have reported that when the Rabi frequency of an ion qubit is close to the servo-bump phase-noise frequency, the driving laser limits the fidelity and coherence time. This issue has typically been mitigated by choosing a Rabi frequency outside the servo-bump region. However, this constrains the usable range of gate speeds and can limit the achievable fidelity. To address this issue, we developed an active phase-noise stabilization system for a barium-ion optical-qubit laser at 1762 nm, employing a fiber electro-optic modulator (EOM) with an electrical feedforward servo. Our results demonstrate that this setup, based on the Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) feedforward method, can suppress servo-bump phase noise by 15 dB near the bump peak frequency in our locking system. The laser phase noise is analyzed using delayed self-heterodyne interferometry (DSHI). We further tested the stabilized laser on an optical qubit and observed a clear improvement in coherence time based on the measured amplitude decay of Rabi oscillations, even when the Rabi frequency lies within the servo-bump bandwidth. This technique can be readily adapted to other optical qubits with minimal modifications.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work proposes using a three-path quantum interferometer to measure the directional chirality of fractional quantum Hall edges. By analyzing interference patterns sensitive to flux and voltage orderings, the authors demonstrate that it is possible to independently extract vertex properties like scaling dimension and exchange angle, which are otherwise conflated in simpler transport measurements.

**Why it may be interesting.** The use of a mesoscopic interferometer setup to probe fundamental topological properties (chirality) in strongly correlated electron systems is highly relevant for understanding edge physics beyond simple Luttinger liquid models.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to test the directional causal response (chirality) of fractional quantum Hall edge excitations and separately determine vertex properties like scaling dimension and exchange angle.

**Main result.** The interferometer setup allows for a measurement that resolves directional causality, providing parameters ($\Delta\ell$ and $	heta_\ell$) that are generally independent when only using standard scaling spectroscopy.

**Method.** Theoretical derivation utilizing the Keldysh formalism to calculate cubic interference kernels in a three-path interferometer geometry. Directionality is isolated by analyzing voltage orderings.

**Model / system.** The system models fractional quantum Hall (FQH) edge excitations ($
u=1/m$) connected via three coherent Quantum Point Contacts (QPCs) forming a flux-enclosing loop. The analysis focuses on the interference between direct and two-step quasiparticle tunneling paths.

**Key observables.** Directional current amplitudes ($A^u_\ell, A^d_\ell$), relative phase ($\Delta\varphi_a$), scaling dimension exponent ($\Delta\ell$), and exchange angle ($	heta_\ell$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Filling factor $
u$, magnetic flux $\Phi$ (via AB harmonics), tunneling weights ($\delta_+$, $\delta_-$), and the ratio of amplitudes $r_\ell$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes low temperature, unresolved delay regimes, and fixed-point universality for the vertex properties.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the cyclic three-path interferometer geometry. Figure 2 compares direct vs. two-step transition amplitudes for downstream and upstream paths contributing to the fundamental AB harmonic.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from deriving the general cubic interference kernel using Keldysh formalism, separating contributions into directional kernels ($I_d^a$ and $I_u^a$), and finally relating these measured ratios/phases back to the intrinsic vertex parameters ($\Delta\ell, 	heta_\ell$).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose an average-current interferometer for the directional causal response of fractional quantum Hall edges. Three coherent quantum point contacts (QPCs) form a flux-enclosing loop, so the leading Aharonov-Bohm harmonic is cubic in tunneling. Interference between a direct transfer and a coherent two-step path resolves downstream and upstream propagation. For a local Laughlin edge at $ν=1/m$, the upstream coefficient vanishes exactly, while the downstream amplitude scales as $E^{3ν-2}$. A weak finite-range nonlocal density interaction spanning the tunneling points activates the upstream coefficient without creating an upstream mode. At low temperature and unresolved delay, its amplitude scales as $E^{2ν-1}$ and its aligned phase relative to the downstream reference is $-π(1-ν)/2+χ_a$ modulo $2π$, with $χ_a=0$ or $π$. Opposite cyclic voltage orderings isolate the two directions, while a folded same-filling Laughlin edge with a neutral weak link realizes a sign-tunable bridge. For a general Abelian edge, the device probes the directional content of the selected tunneling vertex. If $δ_\pm$ are its downstream and upstream weights, its nonzero directional amplitudes scale as $E^{3Δ_\ell-2}$, with $Δ_\ell=δ_++δ_-$, and obey $A^u_\ell/A^d_\ell=|\sin(πδ_-)/\sin(πδ_+)|$. When both are nonzero, positive-flux alignment gives, after removal of a known fixed sign, the relative phase $πΔ_\ell=2πh_\ell$. In the same-vertex coherent unresolved-flight regime, the scaling dimension and directional ratio determine the exchange angle $θ_\ell=π(δ_+-δ_-)$ modulo $2π$. The Aharonov-Bohm flux frequency additionally gives the charge, enabling separate extraction of quasiparticle charge, scaling dimension, and exchange angle.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously solves the two-copy distillability problem for Werner states by deriving a sharp, dimension-free inequality. It extends this analysis to arbitrary copies ($k$), establishing concrete polynomial bounds that define the threshold for $k$-copy undistillability. The work provides deep theoretical insights into entanglement measures using advanced operator inequalities.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on entanglement theory rather than AMO Hamiltonians, the rigorous mathematical techniques involving positive maps, partial traces, and bounding operators are highly relevant to characterizing quantum correlations in many-body systems studied in AMO physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the distillability of Werner states ($ho_\alpha$) when multiple copies are available, aiming to find sharp, dimension-free criteria for $k$-copy undistillability.

**Main result.** They established that $ho_\alpha$ is two-copy distillable if and only if $\alpha < -1/2$, and derived explicit polynomial bounds ($\alpha \ge -\gamma_k$) guaranteeing $k$-copy undistillability for arbitrary $k$.

**Method.** The work employs advanced techniques involving sharp partial-trace inequalities, operator theory (e.g., double-skew Ky Fan bound), and the formulation of necessary conditions via positive operator hierarchies ($H_k(\psi) \succeq 0$).

**Model / system.** The study focuses on Werner states $ho_\alpha$ defined on a bipartite system $C^d \otimes C^d$, analyzed within the framework of quantum information theory, specifically concerning entanglement measures like distillability.

**Key observables.** Distillability criterion ($q_k(\alpha, C) < 0$), operator inequalities ($H_k(\psi) \succeq 0$), and the state parameter $\alpha$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of copies $k$, the local dimension $d$, and the threshold constant $\gamma_k$ which quantifies the boundary between distillable and undistillable states.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary limitation noted is that the general conjecture for all $k \ge 3$ remains unproven, as partial trace does not generally preserve rank-two properties across tensor products.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first solving the two-copy case using a sharp inequality, then generalizing this to arbitrary $k$ via operator hierarchies and polynomial bounds derived from complementary bipartite inequalities, while constantly comparing results against known limitations in tensor product structures.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We solve the two-copy distillability problem for Werner states in every local dimension. Our main matrix result is a sharp, dimension-free inequality: for every rank-at-most-two operator, the sum of the squared Hilbert--Schmidt norms of its two partial traces is bounded by twice its squared Hilbert--Schmidt norm plus one half of the squared modulus of its trace. This implies that a Werner state $ρ_α$ is two-copy distillable if and only if $α<-1/2$. In particular, the two-ququart state $ρ^{(4)}_{-1/2}$ is two-copy undistillable, resolving Problem 5 of Horodecki, Rudnicki, and Życzkowski. For an arbitrary finite number $k$ of copies, we give three exact formulations of the remaining problem. At the endpoint $α=-1/2$, undistillability is equivalent to nonnegativity of the endpoint partial-trace form on every rank-at-most-two operator. We also derive an equivalent hierarchy of operator inequalities $H_k(ψ)\succeq0$ for pure states with a maximally mixed qubit marginal. The two-copy proof does not formally induct, because partial trace can increase rank and $2$-positivity is not generally preserved by tensor products. We prove two rigorous many-copy extensions. First, the quadratic form factorizes exactly on tensor-factorized witnesses; for any such decomposition, the endpoint inequality holds if its possible rank-two factor is supported on a block containing at most two copies. Second, we construct explicit constants $γ_k>0$ such that $α\ge-γ_k$ implies $k$-copy undistillability in every dimension. The initial proofs were generated by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol; the authors have verified and rewritten them to enhance readability and provide additional context.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a novel gradient-based method to design two-body interactions that force an electron system into a desired non-Abelian topological state, specifically the Moore-Read Pfaffian phase. By optimizing pseudopotentials against the known ground state overlap, they achieve near-perfect stabilization of this exotic quantum order. This framework offers a general tool for engineering complex many-body physics using only local interaction terms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, generalizable computational methodology—inverse Hamiltonian design—to engineer exotic topological order in theoretical models relevant to quantum simulation platforms like cold atoms or superconducting circuits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central challenge addressed is engineering specific two-body interactions capable of stabilizing non-Abelian fractional quantum Hall (FQH) phases, such as the Moore-Read Pfaffian state.

**Main result.** The authors successfully designed a pseudopotential profile using gradient optimization that achieves overlaps exceeding 99% with the target Pfaffian ground state for small electron numbers. This demonstrates encoding complex three-body physics into simple two-body interactions.

**Method.** They employed an inverse Hamiltonian design framework, optimizing Haldane pseudopotentials by minimizing the loss function based on the overlap between the system's calculated ground state and the known target Pfaffian wave function.

**Model / system.** The model considers fully spin-polarized electrons confined to a sphere (Haldane geometry) under a magnetic monopole, simulating strongly correlated topological matter at fractional filling ($
u=5/2$).

**Key observables.** Pfaffian overlap ($|\langle \Psi_{	ext{MR}} | \Psi_0 angle|$), neutral excitation spectrum, and Orbital Entanglement Spectrum (OES).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The optimization is constrained by ensuring short-range, repulsive interactions via constraints on the pseudopotentials $\{V_m\}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the ground state remains non-degenerate during the gradient-based optimization process.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare optimized vs. Coulomb pseudopotentials (Fig 2), show excitation spectra and OES confirming Pfaffian/anti-Pfaffian character (Figs 3, 4, 5, 10), and illustrate the exponential decay of optimized potentials with system size (Fig 6).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the inverse design framework using JAX for optimization. It details the overlap maximization procedure, validates the results using spectral diagnostics (OES/TEE), and concludes by identifying a universal, exponentially decaying pseudopotential profile.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Engineering interactions that stabilize non-Abelian fractional quantum Hall phases is a central challenge in strongly correlated topological matter and quantum simulation. We introduce a differentiable framework for inverse Hamiltonian design, in which Haldane pseudopotentials are optimized by gradient-based exact diagonalization to stabilize target fractional quantum Hall phases. In spherical geometry, the Haldane pseudopotentials are treated as variational parameters and optimized in a JAX-based exact-diagonalization framework. By directly maximizing the overlap between the many-body ground state and the Moore-Read state, we obtain a robust pseudopotential profile that has Pfaffian overlaps exceeding $99\%$ for systems up to $N_e=12$, substantially improving over conventional Coulomb interactions. Analyses of the neutral excitation spectrum and orbital entanglement spectrum further confirm that the optimized interaction stabilizes the Pfaffian topological phase. Our results demonstrate that essential features of the three-body Pfaffian parent Hamiltonian can be effectively encoded in a suitably designed two-body interaction. Furthermore, they identify a nearly universal exponentially decaying pseudopotential profile that stabilizes the Pfaffian phase and establishes a general framework toward engineering non-Abelian topological order in quantum simulation.

</details>
