**Summary.** This work uses molecular dynamics simulations on Li2SO4 to characterize the coupling between lithium ion translation and sulfate anion rotation. By varying component masses using VISMD, the authors demonstrate a clear bidirectional coupling mechanism between these two distinct diffusive modes. This finding provides deep insight into how structural dynamics govern ionic conductivity in solid electrolytes.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on ionic solids, the rigorous mathematical framework developed to relate temperature-dependent Arrhenius behavior to power-law scaling exponents (Chunk 4) provides general tools for analyzing coupled dynamics in complex many-body systems, which has parallels in understanding quantum phase transitions or correlated disorder effects.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the coupling mechanism between cation translational dynamics and anion rotational dynamics within solid electrolytes.

**Main result.** The simulations reveal a bidirectional, mode-coupling relationship between the two types of diffusion, suggesting that changes in one dynamic process influence the other.

**Method.** Virtual Isotopic Substitution Molecular Dynamics (VISMD) is employed to independently vary component masses and thus control individual diffusivity rates while preserving the underlying potential energy landscape.

**Model / system.** The model system is alpha-Li2SO4, an archetypal rotor-phase solid electrolyte. The analysis focuses on the interplay between Li+ cation translation and SO4 2- anion rotation.

**Key observables.** Lithium translational diffusivity (D_Li^tr), sulfate rotational diffusivity (D_SO4^rot), power-law scaling exponents, and apparent activation energy for diffusion.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature range (800 K to 1400 K), mass variation factors (varying Li and O masses), and the coupling strength parameter derived from comparing Arrhenius vs. power-law fits.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The VISMD approach assumes that varying atomic masses while keeping potential parameters constant allows for a meaningful, controlled investigation of dynamic mode interplay.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the structure, the power-law scaling of both diffusivities with component mass, and how the apparent activation energy depends on isotopic substitution, confirming coupling effects.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical problem (coupling in solid electrolytes), details the VISMD methodology for controlling individual diffusion modes, presents results showing bidirectional coupling via mass dependence analysis, and concludes by analyzing the implications of this coupling on activation energies.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We characterise the interplay between cation-translational and anion-rotational dynamics on the model system $\rm α\text{-}Li_{2}SO_{4}$ through virtual isotopic substitution molecular dynamics (VISMD) simulations. We independently control in turn the lithium translational- and sufate rotational- diffusivity by varying the masses of lithium and oxygen, respectively, showing that both diffusivities exhibit power-law relationships with the masses of each individual component. Changing either diffusivity produces an effect on the other; i.e. there exists a bidirectional coupling between anion and cation diffusive dynamics. From our variable-temperature/variable-mass dataset we demonstrate that the apparent activation energy for lithium diffusion depends strongly on the isotope mass, decreasing with accelerated sulfate dynamics; an observation which provides clear evidence of mode-coupling between cation and anion dynamics.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a theoretical framework to predict extreme epidemic risk by modeling non-Markovian spreading on complex networks. The core innovation is mapping the system's complex waiting-time statistics onto an equivalent, simpler Markovian process. This allows for quantitative prediction of outbreak size distributions even when infection and recovery times are not exponentially distributed.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on epidemiology, the mathematical techniques—mapping complex stochastic processes (non-Markovian) onto simpler, analytically tractable forms (effective Markovian)—are directly applicable to analyzing open quantum systems or non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is determining the full outbreak-size distribution, especially its right tail, for non-Markovian epidemic spreading on complex networks.

**Main result.** The authors show that mapping non-Markovian SIR dynamics to an effective Markovian description allows for quantitative prediction of extreme outbreak risk across diverse network topologies and waiting-time distributions.

**Method.** They map the non-Markovian process to an effective Markovian one using a single edge transmissibility, employing WKB semiclassical theory for large deviations in weakly heterogeneous networks.

**Model / system.** The model is based on SIR epidemic dynamics ($S+I+R=N$) generalized from standard Markovian assumptions to include arbitrary waiting-time distributions (e.g., Gamma) for infection and recovery periods on complex networks.

**Key observables.** Outbreak-size distribution $P(x^*_r)$, mean outbreak fraction ($x^*_r$), conditional standard deviation ($\sigma^*_r$), and the effective per-edge transmissibility ($T$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Infection/recovery shape parameters ($\alpha_{inf}, \alpha_{rec}$), network heterogeneity quantified by $\sigma_k/ar{k}$, and the basic reproduction number $R_0$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theory relies on mapping non-Markovian dynamics to an effective Markovian process; universality holds best for weakly heterogeneous networks, where WKB approximations are applicable.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the dependence of transmissibility ($T$) and deterministic outbreak fractions on shape parameters ($\alpha$), demonstrating universal collapse for weak heterogeneity, while supplementary figures compare results across different network types (ER, Gamma, Hamsterster) showing deviations due to degree correlations.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the mapping from non-Markovian to effective Markovian dynamics. It then analyzes outbreak statistics using WKB theory for weakly heterogeneous cases, before extending the framework to highly correlated networks using bond percolation concepts.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Extreme epidemic risk is controlled by the right tail of the outbreak-size distribution, but this distribution is generally unknown for non-Markovian spreading on networks. Here we determine this distribution by mapping non-Markovian SIR dynamics to an effective Markovian description. We show that arbitrary infection and recovery time statistics can be incorporated through a single edge transmissibility, yielding an effective Markovian process that reproduces the full outbreak-size statistics. For weakly heterogeneous networks, the reduction yields a universal well-mixed semiclassical theory governed by the bond-percolation reproductive number. Outbreak statistics across diverse waiting-time distributions and topologies collapse onto one predictive curve. For highly heterogeneous and empirical networks, the corresponding effective Markovian dynamics on the network captures the complete distribution. Our results provide a direct route from measured waiting-time distributions to quantitative predictions of network-level extreme-outbreak risk.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports experimental evidence for a field-tuned incommensurate fan phase in $	ext{Na}_2	ext{BaCo}(	ext{PO}_4)_2$ using neutron diffraction. By combining this data with theoretical modeling, the authors argue that dipole-dipole interactions are crucial for stabilizing this complex magnetic state. The paper successfully refines the underlying spin Hamiltonian to account for the observed field dependence of the incommensurate propagation vector.

**Why it may be interesting.** The detailed study of how long-range interactions (dipolar coupling) stabilize exotic phases like the fan phase provides insights into emergent quantum magnetism and frustrated lattice models relevant to strongly correlated electron systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to understand the nature of a field-tuned incommensurate fan phase observed in an Ising-like triangular antiferromagnet, which challenges simple theoretical descriptions.

**Main result.** The authors identify this pre-saturation phase as a coplanar fan phase stabilized by dipole-dipole interactions and bond-dependent exchange anisotropy. They propose a refined spin Hamiltonian that successfully reproduces the complex magnetic phase diagram observed experimentally.

**Method.** The research combines single-crystal neutron diffraction experiments with theoretical modeling using semiclassical Linear Spin Wave Theory (LSWT) and mean-field analysis.

**Model / system.** The system is $	ext{Na}_2	ext{BaCo}(	ext{PO}_4)_2$, an Ising-like triangular-lattice antiferromagnet. The physics is modeled by anisotropic Hamiltonians, requiring the inclusion of dipole-dipole couplings and bond-dependent exchange terms beyond simple nearest-neighbor XXZ models.

**Key observables.** Magnetic Bragg peaks with field-dependent incommensurate propagation vectors ($\mathbf{Q}$), particularly showing movement along the hexagonal Brillouin zone boundary from K towards M points.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Applied magnetic field ($H$), temperature (down to 0.05 K), and coupling constants related to exchange anisotropy ($\Delta$) and dipolar interactions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on semiclassical approximations, treating dipole-dipole coupling as a small source of bond-dependent anisotropy, and using nearest-neighbor approximations for long-range interactions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the crystal structure, representative neutron diffraction maps showing varying $q_z$ components across different magnetic phases (I-III), and critically, the continuous movement of a magnetic Bragg peak in Phase IV as a function of applied field H.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from presenting experimental observations of novel incommensurate peaks to developing theoretical frameworks. It first establishes the limitations of simple XXZ models, then incorporates dipolar couplings via LSWT to explain the observed field-dependent fan phase, culminating in a minimal exchange model that reproduces the full magnetic phase diagram.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Using single-crystal neutron diffraction we report the observation of a field-tuned incommensurate phase in a field range just below magnetization saturation in the Ising-like triangular-lattice antiferromagnet Na$_2$BaCo(PO$_4$)$_2$. This phase occurs for magnetic fields applied along the Ising axis and exhibits an in-plane incommensurate propagation vector that moves along the hexagonal Brillouin zone boundary upon varying field, challenging the simple $XXZ$ antiferromagnetic description of the system. Within a semiclassical framework, we successfully identify this pre-saturation phase as a coplanar fan phase and study the role of dipole-dipole interactions and bond-dependent exchange anisotropy in its stabilization mechanism. We additionally present a minimal exchange model including interlayer couplings, which reproduces the complex magnetic phase diagram in field including the observed field-dependence of the incommensurate propagation vector in the fan phase.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces Hyperdeterminant wavefunctions as a powerful, generalized variational method for studying strongly correlated quantum matter. It allows researchers to access fractionalized degrees of freedom crucial for understanding topological phases like FCI and QSLs. The framework provides both theoretical tools (VMPI) and numerical algorithms (PE) to derive effective field theories for these complex systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state correlations, the development of a general variational framework applicable to fractionalized excitations is mathematically rich and could inspire new ways to model complex quantum dynamics in AMO systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing a theoretical framework to microscopically investigate strongly correlated quantum states of matter, particularly those exhibiting fractionalized degrees of freedom.

**Main result.** The authors introduce Hyperdeterminant (Hdet) wavefunctions as a general variational approach that provides access to fractionalized degrees of freedom and yields reliable microscopic effective field theories for systems like FCI and QSLs.

**Method.** The framework utilizes Hdet wavefunctions, which are generalized from Slater determinants, combined with Variational Manifold Path Integral (VMPI) techniques and Projective Expansion (PE) algorithms for numerical simulation.

**Model / system.** The theory is applied to strongly correlated quantum states of matter, specifically modeling Fractional Chern Insulators (FCI) and Quantum Spin Liquids (QSL). The formalism generalizes fermionic parton constructions beyond standard electron degrees of freedom.

**Key observables.** Microscopic effective field theories, Ward identities for gauge fluctuations, and the structure of the fusion tensor defining the Hdet state.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The rank ($r$) of the underlying tensors, which dictates bosonic or fermionic statistics; lattice parameters governing correlation strength.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Simulating generic Hdet wavefunctions is NP-hard, necessitating approximations like PE. The framework assumes a locality structure for physical reasonableness.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the mathematical construction of Hdet states by comparing submatrix selection in Slater determinants versus tensor contraction using the fusion tensor.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically introduces Hdet wavefunctions, establishes their locality structure, demonstrates applications to QSL and FCI models, derives effective theories via VMPI, and concludes with numerical simulation techniques (PE).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We systematically introduce hyperdeterminant wavefunctions as a variational-wavefunction-based theoretical framework for strongly correlated quantum states of matter, together with practical numerical simulation algorithms. This framework generalizes previously known fermionic parton constructions, yields reliable microscopics with intuitive physical pictures, and allows direct access to the fractionalized degrees of freedom together with associated microscopic effective field theories. We demonstrate the applications of this framework to fractional Chern insulators and quantum spin liquids. We comment that the hyperdeterminant states belong to a more general class of variational wavefunctions: the fused Gaussian states.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper offers a novel theoretical framework by relating the artificial 'thermodynamic force' needed in Adaptive Resolution Simulations (AdResS) to the Liouville-type hierarchy governing open quantum systems. By establishing this correspondence, it derives an integral expression for the force, providing new tools to analyze and validate simulations of complex fluids at interfaces.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a deep theoretical grounding for computational techniques used in simulating complex open systems, connecting mesoscopic numerical artifacts (interface forces) to fundamental statistical mechanics principles (Liouville dynamics).

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work reinterprets the artificial 'thermodynamic force' required in Adaptive Resolution Simulations (AdResS) for open systems by mapping it onto the theoretical framework of the Liouville-type hierarchy.

**Main result.** A substantial part of this coupling force can be rigorously framed using the Liouville-type hierarchy, leading to a derived integral expression that allows for parameter dependency analysis and new validation criteria.

**Method.** The authors derive an explicit correspondence between the numerical force correction in AdResS and the source terms ($\Psi_n$, $\Phi_{n+1}^n$) governing particle flux across boundaries in the Liouville-type equation for open systems.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as an open many-particle fluid (e.g., Lennard-Jones fluid) simulated using AdResS, which partitions space into interacting, transition, and tracer regions to handle interfaces.

**Key observables.** Particle number fluctuations, radial distribution functions, the thermodynamic force ($F_{	ext{th}}$), and the average force ($\vec{F}_{	ext{av}}$) exerted by the environment across boundaries.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Simulation parameters include density ($ho$), temperature ($T$), time step size, and the convergence tolerance for the force calculation.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation assumes that the system can be accurately described by mapping to the Liouville hierarchy, and simplifications are made assuming planar geometry and global thermal equilibrium for the environment.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the setup comparison between full-atomistic reference simulations and AdResS setups across different thermodynamic states; other figures detail particle crossing statistics and force convergence.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the AdResS method and the need for a compensating 'thermodynamic force.' It then develops the theoretical mapping to the Liouville-type hierarchy, deriving integral expressions for the average boundary force. Finally, it validates these theoretical claims through detailed simulation studies of an atomistic fluid.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we present a novel perspective on the coupling force employed to compensate the interface artifacts prevalent in adaptive resolution simulations (AdResS) of open many-particle systems. We show that a substantial part of this "thermodynamic force" can be framed in terms of the theoretical model of the Liouville-type hierarchy for open systems. The correspondence is made explicit for the case of a simple atomistic fluid, for which a one-dimensional integral expression is derived. This enables the analysis for dependencies of the thermodynamic force on important simulation parameters, which is taken to inspire both simplifications for the numerical calculation of the thermodynamic force and new criteria for its validation that are adequate to the interfacial nature of the problem. The theoretical claims are then verified in a simulation study of the atomistic supercritical Lennard-Jones fluid at different thermodynamic states.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces an interactive web platform that unifies knot diagram construction, tensor network evaluation via TQFT, and the computation of colored Chern-Simons invariants. It demonstrates that this framework can systematically classify arborescent knots by mapping their topology onto computable quantum invariants. This represents a significant computational advance in topological quantum field theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly about AMO systems, the use of tensor networks (a computational tool) derived from topological field theory provides a powerful analogy for calculating entanglement or correlation functions in quantum many-body systems where local structure dictates global properties.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is classifying knots in 3D space, which becomes computationally intractable as the crossing number increases.

**Main result.** The authors developed a unified web platform that uses Feynman ribbon diagrams (FRDs) and TQFT principles to compute strong knot invariants for arborescent knots up to at least 10 crossings.

**Method.** They map the combinatorial structure of an FRD onto a tensor network calculation, evaluating it using techniques derived from Chern-Simons theory to yield colored quantum invariants.

**Model / system.** The model is Knot Theory, specifically focusing on arborescent knots represented by Feynman ribbon diagrams (FRDs). The underlying physics framework is Topological Quantum Field Theory (TQFT) applied via Chern-Simons theory.

**Key observables.** Colored quantum invariants (Laurent polynomials in q), which must remain invariant under Reidemeister moves, and the knot determinant.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The crossing number of the knot ($c(K)$); the structure parameters defining the two-vertex FRD ($\Gamma(A_1; p_{12}; A_2)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The platform is currently restricted to tree-shaped (arborescent) FRDs, and while the computation engine is general, knot identification relies on matching computed invariants against a finite database.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the relationship between a knot's conventional projection, its representation as an FRD, and its corresponding TQFT tangle structure. Figure 3 details the two-vertex diagram structure.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of knot classification, proposes the TQFT/FRD framework, details the construction of the interactive web platform ('TQFT Knot Explorer'), presents the mathematical machinery for tensor network evaluation, and concludes with results on the completeness of the two-vertex diagram family up to 10 crossings.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present an interactive web platform that unifies the construction Feynman ribbon diagrams (FRDs), the evaluation of higher-rank Chern--Simons knot invariants, and the identification of FRD-like knots at higher crossing numbers. These tree-structured diagrams naturally represent arborescent knots, which we refer to throughout as FRD-like knots. Within a single visual environment, users can construct an FRD as a tensor network, evaluate its associated Chern--Simons invariants, and use the resulting invariant data to distinguish and identify the corresponding knot. To our knowledge, this is the first platform to combine diagrammatic construction, tensor-network evaluation, invariant computation, and knot identification within a unified workflow.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a novel Purcell-engineered hybrid coupler designed to enhance the robustness of CZ gates in superconducting quantum processors. By integrating both coherent interaction engineering (via the transmon coupler) and leakage-selective dissipation (using filter/notch resonators), the authors achieve state-of-the-art gate fidelities while drastically suppressing unwanted energy loss pathways.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses open quantum system dynamics in superconducting circuits by showing how engineered dissipation (the notch/filter) can complement coherent control to achieve higher fidelity gates, which is a key area for AMO physicists studying cavity QED and open systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is developing robust superconducting controlled-Z (CZ) gates by effectively suppressing leakage into non-computational states.

**Main result.** The proposed Purcell-engineered hybrid coupler significantly reduces leakage probability (down to $1.6	imes10^{-3}$) and improves worst-case gate fidelity ($F_{	ext{min}}=99.62\%$) compared to optimized single-coupler designs.

**Method.** The study employs dressed-eigenstate analysis combined with Lindblad master-equation simulations to model the open quantum system dynamics.

**Model / system.** The platform is superconducting qubits (transmons) coupled via a nonlinear transmon coupler, augmented by an engineered subsystem consisting of a Purcell filter and an auxiliary notch resonator. The Hamiltonian describes coherent interactions ($H_{	ext{int}}$), while dissipation is modeled via Lindblad operators.

**Key observables.** Gate fidelity metrics ($F_{	ext{avg}}, F_{	ext{min}}$) and the leakage probability are the key diagnostics used to quantify gate performance.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The architecture's robustness is tested over a broad range of coherence assumptions and device parameters, with optimized values listed in tables.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Analysis assumes fixed operating frequencies for qubits and coupler during the gate operation. The notch mode coupling is treated under an approximation hierarchy ($g_{fn} \gg g_{1n}, g_{2n}$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the schematic of the hybrid coupler, how effective transverse interaction depends on filter frequency, and spectral responses showing engineered dissipation minima near computational transitions.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from identifying the leakage problem to proposing the hybrid architecture. It analyzes coherent interactions using dressed-eigenstates, models dissipation engineering via the coupled filter-notch subsystem, and finally validates performance using master equation simulations across varying parameters.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose a Purcell-engineered notch-filter hybrid coupler for superconducting controlled-$Z$ (CZ) gates that combines coherent interaction engineering with leakage-selective dissipation. The architecture integrates a nonlinear transmon coupler with a coupled Purcell-filter and notch-resonator subsystem, providing additional control over both the coherent interaction pathways and the engineered dissipative environment. The filter branch reshapes the effective interaction pathways, while the notch resonator further tailors the frequency response of the coupled filter network and preserves strong leakage-selective dissipation.   Using dressed-eigenstate analysis together with Lindblad master-equation simulations, we show that the proposed architecture substantially reduces leakage and improves the worst-case computational-state fidelity compared with an optimized single-transmon coupler while remaining robust over a broad range of coherence assumptions and device parameters. The optimized gate achieves $F_{\rm avg}=99.74\%$, $F_{\rm min}=99.62\%$, and a maximum leakage probability of $1.6\times10^{-3}$. These results demonstrate that engineered dissipation complements conventional coherent interaction engineering and provides an additional design degree of freedom for realizing robust, high-fidelity superconducting CZ gates.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces 'response-selected hyperuniformity' for active fluids, arguing that the observable long-range order depends on which components of the driving force the fluid physically responds to. The authors derive a universal crossover scaling law for the transverse-force spectrum, showing that perfect hyperuniformity is only achieved in the idealized zero-residual limit.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical active matter hydrodynamics, the concept of 'response selection' and deriving universal scaling laws from microscopic constraints (like incompressibility) shares conceptual parallels with how quantum response functions are analyzed in many-body physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To characterize a novel form of emergent hyperuniformity in hydrodynamic active matter, moving beyond treating it as a property of prescribed density fields.

**Main result.** The transverse-force spectrum exhibits a universal crossover from fourth- to sixth-order scaling, demonstrating that strict hyperuniformity requires zero residual activity moments.

**Method.** Mathematical derivation using Fourier space analysis and source-response formalism applied to hydrodynamic interactions in an incompressible fluid.

**Model / system.** A reversible valence-one active fluid model involving overdamped carriers with signed first moments, interacting hydrodynamically.

**Key observables.** Transverse-force spectrum $	ilde{\chi}_f^T(\mathbf{k})$, source spectrum $S_1(\mathbf{k})$, and the crossover wave number $k_	imes$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The ratio of unscreened residual to screened analytic contribution, which sets the crossover scale.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes an incompressible fluid response and models the source spectrum as a sum of an analytic (cluster) term and a constant plateau (residual moment).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate active multipoles evolution and display the resulting transverse-force spectra, showing the characteristic crossover behavior.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces response-selected hyperuniformity by analyzing how fluid incompressibility selects specific force components. It derives the spectral form exhibiting a $k^4 	o k^6$ crossover based on residual vs. screened contributions, concluding that finite residuals cause infrared leakage.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hyperuniformity in active matter is usually treated as a property of a prescribed density or continuum field. This view misses a basic feature of hydrodynamic active matter: an incompressible fluid does not respond equally to every microscopic force. Longitudinal forcing is absorbed into pressure, whereas transverse forcing drives flow. The relevant question is therefore not only whether particles are uniformly arranged or whether the total activity is small, but which sector of the active forcing is selected by the physical response. Here we introduce response-selected hyperuniformity, in which long-wavelength order is a property of a source-response pair. In a reversible valence-one fluid with no prescribed partners, locally neutral clusters screen the signed active-moment sector that controls transverse flow, producing a first-moment spectrum that vanishes quadratically at low wavenumber. Locally unscreened moments instead generate a nonzero infrared plateau. The resulting transverse-force spectrum has a universal crossover from fourth- to sixth-order scaling, with the crossover set by the ratio of the unscreened residual to the screened analytic contribution. Complete partner renewal preserves this normal form, establishing exchangeable multipole inheritance, while turnover tunes the residual through an independently measured local defect density. The zero-residual limit yields strictly hyperuniform velocity fluctuations; any finite residual causes defect-controlled infrared leakage and sets a finite screening length. Thus microscopic exchange need not destroy hidden hyperuniform flow order, but rare unscreened moments determine how far the quiet-flow regime survives.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes reformulating quantum mechanics as a 'Theory of Potentiality' using complex-valued measure theory. It distinguishes between the linear mathematics governing unactualized potentialities and the nonlinear Born map that yields observable probabilities. This framework aims to provide a deeper, pre-probabilistic understanding of QM while remaining mathematically equivalent to standard formalism.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work offers a deep conceptual re-foundation of quantum mechanics that addresses the measurement problem by positing an underlying mathematical structure of unresolved potentiality, which is highly relevant to foundational questions in open quantum systems theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To reformulate quantum mechanics (QM) as a fundamental theory of 'unresolved uncertainty' rather than solely focusing on probabilities derived from actualized outcomes.

**Main result.** The proposed potentiality framework is empirically equivalent to standard QM but makes explicit the pre-probabilistic structure underlying quantum phenomena like interference and entanglement.

**Method.** It utilizes complex-valued measure theory, treating potentialities as primary objects that retain linear additivity, contrasting this with the nonlinear Born map required for observable probabilities.

**Model / system.** The model describes general quantum systems using potentiality distributions ($\psi$), which are complex-valued measures over an underlying context space $\Omega$. It systematically maps standard QM concepts (e.g., partial trace, Lüders update) to analogous structures in this new formalism.

**Key observables.** Observable probabilities ($p_X(x)$), coherent potentiality aggregates ($P(A)$), and the structure of joint potentialities ($\psi(x, y)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The distinction between linear (potentiality) and quadratic (probability/Born map) structures is key; no specific physical parameters are emphasized over the mathematical formalism.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is that QM can be fundamentally understood as a theory of pre-probabilistic potentialities, which requires redefining primitive notions away from standard probability axioms.

**Figures summary.** A detailed comparison table maps standard quantum mechanical concepts (e.g., density matrix, Lüders update) to their corresponding structures within the Theory of Potentiality.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically develops a 'potentiality language,' contrasting it with standard QM by defining analogues for core probabilistic operations (conditioning, independence) at the complex measure level before applying the Born map.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose a reformulation of quantum mechanics as a theory of unresolved uncertainty. The framework is formulated in the language of complex-valued measure theory, regarded as a pre-probabilistic counterpart of ordinary probability theory. In this formulation, additivity, conditioning, independence, mixtures, transition kernels, and temporal divisibility retain natural linear forms at the potentiality level, while non-classical probability-level features such as interference arise from the nonlinear Born map. Measurement is described as Bayesian-type conditioning of potentialities on actualized information, and non-selective measurement as the replacement of coherent potentiality by statistical mixtures of conditional branches. Mixed states, decoherence, composite systems, entanglement, and Bell-type correlations are also given a unified potentiality-level interpretation. The resulting formulation is empirically equivalent to standard quantum mechanics, but it makes explicit a pre-probabilistic description of physical reality that is usually implicit in the Hilbert-space formalism.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces Tree Tensor Network Reservoir Computing (TTN-RC), a method for time-series prediction that uses random tree tensors as its reservoir. To ensure stable operation, they propose a hierarchical ensemble structure and derive theoretical stability boundaries using Jacobian analysis. This provides both improved predictive performance and a rigorous design principle based on tensor network physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** While primarily ML-focused, the rigorous mathematical analysis of stability boundaries ($\sigma_T=\sqrt{2}$) and the use of tensor network contractions echo techniques used in analyzing quantum many-body systems and entanglement measures.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing a quantum-inspired reservoir computing framework (TTN-RC) for time-series prediction that addresses the inherent exponential concentration or divergence of outputs in standard Tree Tensor Networks.

**Main result.** The proposed hierarchical ensemble method mitigates instability, and an asymptotic stability boundary is identified at $\sigma_{T}=\sqrt{2}$, providing a design principle for tensor-network-based reservoir computing.

**Method.** The authors combine the use of random Tree Tensor Networks as reservoirs with a novel hierarchical ensemble technique to stabilize the system's dynamics. They employ mean-field theory and Jacobian analysis to derive stability criteria.

**Model / system.** The model is TTN-RC, an extension of Echo State Networks (ESNs) where the reservoir state generation uses a random tree tensor network structure instead of standard weight matrices. The system utilizes $M$ independent sub-reservoirs whose outputs are concatenated.

**Key observables.** Expected contraction rate ($C$), variance of the Jacobian matrix ($V^{(l)}_J$), and performance metrics like $R^2$ on NARMA benchmarks.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Tensor-element standard deviation ($\sigma_T$), total reservoir size ($N_x$), number of sub-reservoirs ($M$), and network depth ($L$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the independence assumption for tensor contractions and assumes that the ensemble structure allows for a mean-field description of stability.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 conceptually illustrates the recursive, tree-like structure used for updating the reservoir state in TTN-RC.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the TTN-RC model and its hierarchical ensemble extension. It then develops theoretical analyses using Jacobian calculations to derive stability criteria (contraction rate) and concludes with experimental validation on time-series prediction tasks.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose Tree Tensor Network Reservoir Computing (TTN-RC), a quantum-inspired reservoir computing framework for time-series prediction that uses the hierarchical structure of Tree Tensor Networks as a random reservoir. To control the exponential concentration or divergence of TTN outputs, we introduce a hierarchical ensemble method that partitions a fixed-size reservoir into multiple independent sub-reservoirs. In the tested NARMA benchmarks, TTN-RC achieves competitive or improved performance compared with conventional Echo State Networks, especially for tasks requiring higher-order nonlinear processing and longer contextual dependence. We also derive an expected contraction rate based on the reservoir Jacobian and develop a mean-field description of the reservoir-state statistics. These analyses identify an asymptotic stability boundary at $σ_{T}=\sqrt{2}$ in the large per-tree-size limit, where several theoretical indicators converge. Our results provide a design principle for tensor-network-based reservoir computing and clarify how hierarchical reservoir topology controls stability and nonlinear information processing.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a comprehensive, noise-aware framework to optimize quantum algorithm execution on current hardware. It derives analytical methods to calculate the minimum necessary number of measurement shots and optimally distributes these shots across circuit partitions. The resulting resource allocation strategy significantly reduces both computational error and energy consumption compared to standard practices.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on computation, the rigorous mathematical treatment of noise accumulation and resource optimization (shot allocation) provides deep insights into the fundamental limits imposed by decoherence in open quantum systems, which is relevant for theoretical modeling of noisy physical platforms.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work addresses determining the optimal number of measurement shots required for reliable quantum algorithm execution and developing a noise-aware method to distribute a fixed shot budget across circuit partitions.

**Main result.** The proposed analytical framework reduces required shots by about 58% (leading to up to 62% energy reduction) and can reduce the total estimation error by up to 73% compared to conventional, non-optimized approaches.

**Method.** It derives closed-form analytical expressions for optimal shot counts and uses Lagrange multipliers to solve a resource allocation problem that minimizes total estimation error subject to fixed budget constraints.

**Model / system.** The analysis is applied to near-term quantum computers characterized by noise, limited gate fidelities, and the need for repeated circuit executions (shots). It models success probability using binomial/normal distributions incorporating hardware noise variance.

**Key observables.** Shots ($s$), Total Estimation Error ($\mathcal{E}$), Energy Consumption, Maximum Executable Depth ($d_{\max}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coherence times ($T_1, T_2$), gate error probability ($p_g$), Circuit Depth ($d$), Target Success Probability ($P(s)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Approximations are made for circuit execution time ($t_{circ} \approx d \cdot t_g$) and the noise variance calculation relies on suppressing higher-order terms in the noise model.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate comparisons of estimation error across different partitioning strategies, show the workflow for shot estimation and depth calculation, and compare energy consumption savings between optimal vs. equal shot allocation.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the need for reliable shots to deriving analytical expressions for required shots, then developing a framework to calculate maximum feasible circuit depth ($d_{\max}$), and finally solving an optimization problem using Lagrange multipliers to optimally allocate shots across partitions to minimize total error.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Any algorithm execution on quantum computers requires several repeated and costly executions (known as shots) to obtain reliable results. In this work, we propose a closed-form accurate analytical expression to determine optimal number of shots required for reliable execution of any algorithm on a quantum computer. We also present a theoretically grounded technique to distribute fixed shot budget across different partitions in a quantum circuit minimizing the total error. Our proposed analytical model helps to reduce the shots associated with reliable execution of quantum algorithms by about 58\% compared to current practice, in turn reducing the energy consumption by upto 62\%. Furthermore, our proposed optimal shot allocation technique across different partitions reduces total error by up to 73\% compared to conventional approaches.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper extends de Finetti theorems by constraining physical states to be fixed points of quantum channels, thereby generalizing symmetry arguments. Using advanced tools from functional analysis and representation theory, the authors derive tight bounds on quantum capacities and provide efficient algorithms for related problems. This work advances the mathematical understanding of correlations in quantum systems under structural constraints.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous mathematical machinery to analyze quantum correlations under symmetry constraints, which is crucial for understanding resource theories in open quantum systems and quantum information processing.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work studies de Finetti hierarchies when quantum states are constrained to be fixed points of quantum channels, generalizing classical symmetry arguments.

**Main result.** They derive several quantitative de Finetti theorems with improved convergence rates and establish efficient computational schemes for related problems like separable inner approximations.

**Method.** The approach combines the mean-ergodic theorem with structure theory of conditional expectations, utilizing algebraic tools from representation theory (Schur-Weyl duality, Gelfand-Tsetlin bases).

**Model / system.** The focus is on quantum statistical processes and density operators constrained by fixed points of quantum channels ($\Phi(ho) = ho$), which subsumes invariance under compact symmetry groups.

**Key observables.** Entanglement-assisted classical capacity, block-wise distortion bounds for measurements, and convergence rates in de Finetti theorems (e.g., $O(\sqrt{\log n}/n)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The local dimension ($d$), the number of subsystems ($n$), and the error tolerance ($\epsilon$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The results rely on adapting information-theoretic proofs to fixed point constraints, effectively treating symmetries as general fixed point conditions.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops tools by first establishing bounds related to conditional expectations and measurements adapted to fixed point algebras. This leads to the derivation of refined de Finetti theorems (double-sided extension, interpolation) and concludes with applications to optimization and error correction.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

De Finetti theorems convert permutation symmetry into approximate mixtures of product states and thereby justify a wide range of reductions in classical and quantum statistics. In this work we study de Finetti hierarchies in which the feasible states are additionally constrained to be fixed points of quantum channels, a condition that subsumes invariance under arbitrary compact symmetry groups. Combining the mean-ergodic theorem with the structure theory of conditional expectations, we prove a tight bound on the entanglement-assisted classical capacity of the dual of a conditional expectation, block-wise distortion bounds for informationally complete measurements adapted to fixed point algebras, and an exact type-based refinement of the chain rule for permutation-invariant states. From these tools we derive several de Finetti theorems: a double-sided extension theorem with $O\left(\sqrt{\log n}/n\right)$ convergence, an interpolation theorem whose dimension dependence is governed solely by the block structure of the fixed point algebras and which recovers the dimension-independent classical behavior for maximal tori, and a Bose-symmetric variant. Exploiting Schur-Weyl duality and Gelfand-Tsetlin bases, we further show that the rounding scheme producing certifiably good separable inner approximations for (constrained) separability problems can be implemented in time polynomial in $1/ε$ for fixed local dimensions, complementing the known efficient outer hierarchies. Applications to bilinear optimization under symmetries and to approximate quantum error correction are discussed.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes how optical loss and photon indistinguishability affect generating entangled states using Gaussian resources in photonics. By developing a numerical optimization framework, the authors show that while these imperfections degrade efficiency, fidelity remains high if non-Gaussian operations are strategically employed alongside post-selection. This offers crucial guidelines for building robust quantum photonic circuits.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides practical design guidelines for scalable quantum state engineering on integrated photonic platforms by quantifying the impact of unavoidable experimental imperfections like loss and distinguishability.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study quantitatively investigates how optical loss and photon distinguishability degrade the heralded generation of entangled quantum states using Gaussian resources.

**Main result.** Non-Gaussian operations, combined with non-vacuum post-selection, can enhance state generation performance under realistic imperfections, showing that losses primarily reduce success probability rather than fundamentally compromising fidelity.

**Method.** An efficient numerical framework in a phase-space representation is established to optimize target-state fidelity and success probability by incorporating mode-dependent loss and partial distinguishability statistics.

**Model / system.** The system models heralded entanglement generation using multi-mode Gaussian sources (squeezed states) directed through an interferometer, subject to linear loss channels ($\eta$) and modeled photon distinguishability components.

**Key observables.** Target-state fidelity ($F$), success probability ($P$), and the trade-off between these two observables mapped via Pareto frontiers.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Squeezing parameters, interferometer tuning parameters, optical loss rate ($\eta$), and the degree of photon distinguishability.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis treats the system using a combination of Gaussian operations and an approximation for partial distinguishability; post-selection strategies are used to mitigate vacuum noise.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the dependence of $P$ and $F$ on loss rates ($\eta$) and non-Gaussian operation counts, showing Pareto frontiers mapping the trade-off between fidelity and success probability for Bell, GHZ, and W states.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the model incorporating loss and distinguishability, then optimizing system parameters (squeezing/interferometer) using numerical methods, and finally demonstrating performance enhancement via non-Gaussian operations and post-selection.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The effects of optical loss and photon distinguishability on the heralded generation of entangled states based on Gaussian resources are quantitatively investigated. By incorporating mode-dependent loss and the statistical characteristics of partially distinguishable photons into a phase-space representation, an efficient numerical framework is established to optimize target-state fidelity and success probability, with a specific focus on the enhancement triggered by non-Gaussian operations such as photon addition and subtraction. The numerical optimization results indicate that a non-vacuum post-selection strategy within a dual-rail encoding framework, combined with the simultaneous tuning of squeezing parameters and the interferometer network, effectively suppresses vacuum noise, enabling the generation of high-fidelity Bell, GHZ, and W states under realistic experimental constraints. The results show that introducing non-Gaussian operations can successfully enhance the state generation performance under realistic imperfections analogous to the enhancements observed under ideal conditions. This study demonstrates that experimental imperfections primarily scale down the success probability rather than fundamentally compromising the state fidelity, providing practical design guidelines for scalable state engineering on integrated photonic platforms.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports the synthesis and characterization of $1T-	ext{CrS}_2$, demonstrating it as a promising layered magnet. The research combines experimental transport measurements showing topological effects with sophisticated theoretical calculations that prove these phenomena arise from the cooperative action of electronic correlations and spin-orbit coupling in this correlated material.

**Why it may be interesting.** The interplay between strong electron correlations (Hubbard physics), spin-orbit coupling, and emergent topology is central to modern condensed matter theory, making this highly relevant for understanding correlated materials beyond simple band theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge is realizing a single 2D platform that robustly integrates correlated magnetism, electronic topology, and transport phenomena in layered magnets.

**Main result.** The study establishes $1T-	ext{CrS}_2$ as a rare correlated 3d layered ferromagnet where electronic correlations and spin-orbit coupling cooperatively drive emergent topological transport.

**Method.** A combination of experimental techniques (CVD growth, transport/magnetization measurements) and advanced theoretical calculations ($	ext{DFT}+U+	ext{SOC}$, Heisenberg exchange) was employed.

**Model / system.** The physical system is layered $1T-	ext{CrS}_2$, a transition-metal dichalcogenide known for its octahedral coordination, which promotes strong electron correlations and intrinsic magnetism.

**Key observables.** Robust ferromagnetism with out-of-plane easy-axis anisotropy; semimetal–insulator crossover near 80 K; topological Hall effect below 30 K; gap opening upon inclusion of SOC/correlations.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Curie temperature ($T_C$) above room temperature; low temperatures ($	ext{T} < 30	ext{ K}$) for topological effects; correlation strength ($U$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The study assumes the stability and synthesizability of the $1T$ polymorph via CVD, and uses theoretical models (like $\Delta_\alpha(T)$) to describe temperature-dependent crossovers.

**Figures summary.** Figures show crystal structures, temperature dependence of resistance revealing a crossover, calculated spectral functions comparing DFT vs. SOC vs. correlated methods, and 2D Fermi surface projections under different theoretical treatments.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first reporting the synthesis (CVD) and basic magnetic/transport measurements. It then uses advanced electronic structure calculations ($	ext{DFT} 	o 	ext{DFT}+	ext{SOC} 	o 	ext{DFT}+U+	ext{SOC}$) to explain the observed phenomena, culminating in a unified picture of correlation-driven topological transport.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The realization of correlated layered magnets hosting robust ferromagnetism with emergent topological transport remains a key challenge in quantum materials. Here we report the first catalyst-free chemical vapour deposition growth of layered 1T-CrS$_2$, establishing a highly stable vdWs ferromagnet with an out-of-plane easy-axis anisotropy and a Curie temperature above room temperature. Transport measurements reveal a semimetal--insulator crossover near 80 K and pronounced negative magnetoresistance up to 350 K. A topological Hall effect emerges below 30 K, a rare signature of correlated transport in layered transition-metal dichalcogenide ferromagnets. First-principles calculations show that spin--orbit coupling gaps Dirac-like crossings, while electronic correlations reconstruct the Fermi surface by suppressing electron pockets and reducing the carrier density, enhancing momentum-dependent out-of-plane spin polarization. Magnetic measurements, supported by Heisenberg exchange calculations, reveal strong nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic exchange that stabilizes long-range ferromagnetism. Our results establish 1T-CrS$_2$ as a rare correlated 3$d$ layered ferromagnet in which electronic correlations and spin--orbit coupling cooperatively drive emergent topological transport.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study analyzes the bilayer Hubbard model, showing that superconducting pairing is optimally enhanced near a Mott Insulator–Band Insulator crossover. This enhancement mechanism is driven by the cooperative development of low-energy self-energy poles in both electronic bands. The work demonstrates that interlayer hopping ($t_\perp$) acts as a tunable knob to control this exotic pairing mechanism.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of using controllable parameters ($t_\perp$) to tune emergent fermionic excitations (self-energy poles) for optimizing superconductivity is highly relevant to understanding engineered quantum materials and strongly correlated physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how the real-frequency structure of the self-energy dictates superconductivity enhancement in the bilayer Hubbard model.

**Main result.** Superconductivity is maximized near the Mott Insulator–Band Insulator (MI–BI) crossover boundary, where low-energy self-energy poles from both bands cooperatively enhance $s^{\pm}$-wave pairing.

**Method.** The research employs the Dynamical Cluster Approximation (DCA) combined with an equation of motion approach to analyze spectral functions and self-energies.

**Model / system.** The system is the bilayer Hubbard model on a square lattice, described by hopping parameters ($t, t_\perp$) and onsite repulsion ($U$). The analysis focuses on bonding ($eta$) and antibonding ($\alpha$) bands.

**Key observables.** Self-energy poles (real-frequency structure), superconducting order parameter ($\Delta$), band-selective pseudogaps, and the excitation gap $\Delta$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interlayer hopping ($t_\perp$), onsite repulsion ($U$), doping level ($\delta=0.02$ to $0.05$), and the MI–BI crossover boundary.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on interpreting self-energies via a 'hidden-fermion model' which successfully captures pole structure across the crossover, although this ansatz fails at higher doping levels.

**Figures summary.** Figures map out superconducting order parameters in $(U, t_\perp)$ planes, showing maxima near the MI–BI boundary. Other figures illustrate spectral functions and self-energy evolution during the MI–BI crossover via pole crossing.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the self-energy poles across doping regimes ($\delta=0$ to $\delta=0.05$) and varying $t_\perp$. It first establishes the MI–BI crossover mechanism, then uses this structure to explain enhanced pairing, culminating in mapping out phase boundaries.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the real-frequency structure of the self-energy in the bilayer Hubbard model, using the dynamical cluster approximation. At half filling, the Mott insulator-band insulator (MI-BI) crossover involves a rearrangement of self-energy poles between the bonding and antibonding bands; these poles cross as the interlayer hopping $t_{\perp}$ is varied. Upon doping, this pole structure produces a band-selective pseudogap and enhances $s^{\pm}$-wave superconductivity. The order parameter is maximized near the MI-BI boundary, where low-energy anomalous self-energy poles develop simultaneously in both bands and cooperatively enhance the pairing. We further show that these self-energy poles can be interpreted as emergent fermionic excitations, offering an enhanced-pairing mechanism in common with the single-layer Hubbard model. The controllability of these poles through $t_{\perp}$ makes the bilayer system an unconventional platform for optimizing strongly correlated superconductivity.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel basis optimization technique to alleviate the sign problem plaguing Quantum Monte Carlo simulations. By systematically rotating the local Hilbert space basis based on minimizing non-stoquasticity, the authors achieve improved simulation accuracy and reach lower temperatures for frustrated magnetic models. This provides a powerful new computational tool for studying strongly correlated quantum matter.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the core methodology—systematic numerical optimization of simulation representations using advanced gradient descent techniques—is highly relevant to developing robust computational tools for complex quantum systems in AMO physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is the sign problem in Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations, which causes exponential statistical fluctuations for certain quantum many-body systems.

**Main result.** The authors developed a basis optimization technique that significantly mitigates the sign problem by rotating the local Hilbert space basis, enabling simulations at lower temperatures than previous state-of-the-art methods.

**Method.** The method involves optimizing the local basis via unitary rotations, guided by minimizing a generalized non-stoquasticity measure ($S(U)$), which is hypothesized to coincide with maximizing the average sign ($\langle s angle$).

**Model / system.** The approach is benchmarked on frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets on lattices such as the one-dimensional chain, the two-dimensional maple-leaf lattice (MLL), and ladder systems.

**Key observables.** Average Sign ($\langle s angle$), Non-stoquasticity ($S(U)$), Specific Heat Capacity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$) and various coupling strengths defining the magnetic interactions ($J$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The optimization relies on the assumption that minimizing non-stoquasticity guides the system toward maximizing the average sign, although this is noted to be a sufficient but not necessary condition for solving the problem.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate computational phase diagrams showing optimal basis changes across coupling strengths (MLL), and plots comparing $\langle s angle$ versus $S(U)$ for different ladder systems.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the sign problem in SSE-QMC to proposing a general unitary basis rotation scheme, detailing the two-stage optimization process (Adam/LBFGS), and finally benchmarking this technique on specific frustrated lattice models.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The sign problem breaks the polynomial scaling of Quantum Monte Carlo methods. We alleviate it by rotation of the local basis of the Hilbert space, such that the phase of off-diagonal matrix elements of the rotated Hamiltonian is minimized. These minima coincide with optima of the average sign. We benchmark our method for frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets in one dimension and on the two-dimensional maple-leaf lattice. Our approach reveals more efficient bases with improved sign in a large part of the parameter space for all models considered, enabling us to reach lower temperatures, on par with state-of-the-art numerical linked cluster expansions which we directly compare to.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically investigates how best to estimate both the phase and coherence of light collected by astronomical interferometers. It compares two methods—direct measurement versus quantum teleportation—and finds that direct interferometry is generally superior, though the optimal method depends on the baseline length. The work establishes key theoretical bounds for achievable estimation precision.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly applies advanced quantum estimation theory to a fundamental problem in astrophysics (interferometry), providing quantitative comparisons between different quantum measurement protocols for parameter estimation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is the simultaneous estimation of both the relative phase ($\phi$) and the degree of coherence ($\mu$ or $\gamma$) in astronomical interferometry, as joint recovery is necessary for true imaging.

**Main result.** The direct interferometry scheme consistently achieves a lower Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound (QCRB) compared to the continuous-variable quantum teleportation scheme. Furthermore, performance depends on baseline length: direct methods are better for short baselines, while teleportation excels at long baselines.

**Method.** The analysis uses Gaussian multiparameter quantum estimation theory, comparing the Classical and Quantum Fisher Information Matrices (CRB vs QCRB) derived for two distinct measurement schemes.

**Model / system.** The physical system is astronomical interferometry using separated telescopes to measure light coherence. The theoretical models compared are the direct interferometry scheme and a continuous-variable quantum teleportation scheme utilizing squeezed vacuum states.

**Key observables.** Relative phase ($\phi$), degree of coherence ($\gamma$ or $\mu$), Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound (QCRB), and Classical Cramér-Rao Bound (CRB).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Total mean photon number ($\epsilon$), transmissivity ($T$), baseline length ($L$), and the coherence parameter ($\gamma$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on Gaussian measurement theory, and specific comparisons are made under assumptions regarding transmission loss coefficients.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare QCRB vs. photon number ($\epsilon$) for different coherences ($\gamma$); they also plot the optimized difference between CRB and QCRB, and show a crossover behavior in performance versus baseline length ($L$).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the joint estimation problem, develops theoretical frameworks for both direct interferometry and quantum teleportation schemes using Fisher information matrices, derives and compare the resulting QCRBs, and finally analyzes the dependence of precision on environmental factors like transmission loss and baseline distance.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Astronomical interferometry is a cornerstone technique for high-resolution stellar imaging and observational astrophysics, extracting spatial information from the coherence of light collected by separated telescopes. Since the degree of coherence is complex, a genuine imaging task requires the joint recovery of the modulus and the relative phase, instead of independent singleparameter estimations. We investigate the simultaneous estimation of both parameters based on direct interferometry scheme and continuou-svariable quantum teleportation scheme. We find that in simultaneous estimation the direct interferometry scheme consistently yields a lower quantum Cramér-Rao bound, demonstrating its superiority over the continuous-variable quantum teleportation scheme. Furthermore, we establish the conditions under which the classical Cramér-Rao bound for Gaussian measurements saturates the quantum Cramér-Rao bound, identifying heterodyne detection as a near-optimal measurement scheme in the large mean photon number regime. An analysis of transmission loss reveals that the direct interferometry scheme yields superior precision in the short-baseline regime, whereas the continuous-variable quantum teleportation scheme outperforms it at longer baselines.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports on single crystals of $	ext{CeZn}_{2-x}	ext{Ga}_{2+x}$, finding that the material exhibits complex magnetism, including metamagnetic transitions. The key finding is that local structural disorder at the Ce site drives competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic correlations, leading to spin glass behavior. This demonstrates a method for engineering frustrated magnetic states by controlling crystallographic imperfections.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides an experimental demonstration of how engineering lattice disorder can tune competing magnetic interactions (FM/AFM), a concept highly relevant for designing novel quantum materials with tailored magnetic ground states.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the structural and magnetic properties of $	ext{CeZn}_{2-x}	ext{Ga}_{2+x}$ to understand how tuning local crystallographic disorder influences complex magnetic states.

**Main result.** The material exhibits distinct magnetic transitions ($\sim 4 	ext{ K}$) and metamagnetic states, which are attributed to positional disorder at the Ce site driving competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic correlations, leading to spin glass behavior.

**Method.** The research combines single crystal growth, transport measurements (resistivity, heat capacity), and advanced structural analysis using neutron powder diffraction coupled with Reverse Monte Carlo simulations.

**Model / system.** The physical system is the $	ext{R-Zn-Ga}$ intermetallic family, specifically $	ext{CeZn}_{2-x}	ext{Ga}_{2+x}$, which adopts a tetragonal $	ext{BaAl}_4$ ($	ext{I}4/	ext{mmm}$) parent structure. The focus is on how local disorder affects the magnetic interactions within this crystalline lattice.

**Key observables.** Magnetic transition temperature ($\sim 4 	ext{ K}$), metamagnetic states, strong magnetic anisotropy, and evidence of local crystallographic disorder at the Ce site (from RMC analysis).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$), applied magnetic field ($H$), and stoichiometry variations ($x$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The complex magnetism observed is driven by positional disorder of the Ce atom, rather than just $	ext{Zn}/	ext{Ga}$ site disorder.

**Figures summary.** Figures show X-ray/neutron diffraction data used for structural refinement and RMC analysis; other figures present magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$) and heat capacity ($C_p$) vs. $T$ curves demonstrating the transitions.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by characterizing the crystal structure via multiple diffraction techniques, establishing the presence of magnetic features through transport measurements, and finally using advanced RMC analysis on neutron data to link the observed magnetism directly to local structural disorder.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The tetragonal BaAl$_4$ ($I4/mmm$) parent structure underpins a diverse family of materials exhibiting novel phenomena, including nematic superconductivity, topological semimetallicity, and heavy fermion behavior. The recent growth of ternary R-Zn-Ga compounds, such as the previously reported CeZn$_2$Ga$_2$, has explored some of the members exhibiting rare-earth magnetism within this family. In this paper, we report on the structural and magnetic properties of single crystals of CeZn$_{2-x}$Ga$_{2+x}$, a Ga-rich analogue of CeZn$_2$Ga$_2$. Our CeZn$_{2-x}$Ga$_{2+x}$ samples exhibit magnetic properties distinct from the paramagnetic behavior previously reported for CeZn$_2$Ga$_2$. We observe a magnetic transition around 4 K, pronounced metamagnetic states at low temperatures, and strong magnetic anisotropy. Though there are batch-to-batch variations that suggest a strong sensitivity to local structural imperfections, we consistently see the presence of magnetic transitions and metamagnetic states in our crystals. To investigate the local structural sensitivity hypothesis, we performed Reverse Monte Carlo analysis of collected powder neutron diffraction data, revealing the presence of significant local crystallographic disorder of the magnetic Ce site. Our findings demonstrate that the positional disorder drives competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic correlations that lead to the observed spin glass behavior and complex anisotropic magnetism. This study illustrates that tuning the local crystallographic disorder enables engineering frustrated magnetic states in BaAl$_4$-type and similar intermetallic structures.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a structural theory for Approximate Quantum Error Correction (AQEC) by generalizing the successful error-set model from exact QEC. It shows that while full linearity fails in the approximate regime, a restricted form suffices to define uniform performance guarantees using new metrics like environment-leakage distance. This advances the field by providing general tools applicable across diverse quantum physical systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a powerful, general mathematical framework for analyzing noise resilience in quantum systems beyond simple channel-by-channel analysis, directly impacting how we design fault-tolerant protocols for platforms like Rydberg arrays or fermionic qubits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to develop a structural theory for Approximate Quantum Error Correction (AQEC) that mirrors the robust error-set formulation available for exact QEC.

**Main result.** The authors establish a restricted form of Knill–Laflamme linearity sufficient for AQEC, deriving uniform fidelity guarantees using new parameters like the environment-leakage distance and the Knill-Laflamme Hellinger distance.

**Method.** The methodology involves extending the error-set model by analyzing families of channels whose Kraus operators are linear combinations of a fixed error set under spectral constraints. This utilizes both worst-case (Bény-Oreshkov) and average-case (Petz) frameworks.

**Model / system.** The theory is applied to general quantum systems, developing constructions for fermionic systems, one-dimensional Rydberg-blockaded systems, and deletion errors, placing exact and approximate correction on equal footing.

**Key observables.** Fidelity guarantees, environment-leakage distance, Knill-Laflamme Hellinger distance, code distance.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Approximation parameter $\epsilon$, error set $\mathcal{E}$, spectral constraint norms ($\|C\|_\infty$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is that a restricted form of linearity survives the transition from exact to approximate QEC. The analysis also uses Bény-Oreshkov and Petz average-case frameworks.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first identifying the structural gap between exact and approximate QEC, then proposing the restricted error-set model governed by spectral constraints. It details the derivation of new fidelity guarantees using worst-case and average-case metrics before presenting diverse physical constructions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a theory of approximate quantum error correction (QEC) based on the error-set model, complemented by general methods for code construction. Exact QEC has a powerful error-set structure: by the Knill-Laflamme conditions, a code correcting a given error set automatically protects against every channel whose Kraus operators lie in their linear span. This linearity gives rise to code distance, the equivalence between erasures and general errors, and a theory of asymptotically good codes. A longstanding view has been that these features do not extend to AQEC, leaving the theory essentially channel-by-channel. We show instead that, although full Knill--Laflamme linearity fails, a restricted form survives and suffices to extend all three structural features to the approximate setting. Specifically, a common error-set criterion governs families of channels whose Kraus operators are linear combinations of a given error set and whose coefficient matrices satisfy a spectral constraint. Using the Bény-Oreshkov worst-case and Petz average-case frameworks, we derive uniform fidelity guarantees for these families in terms of two new code parameters--the \emph{environment-leakage distance}, controlling worst-case performance, and the \emph{Knill-Laflamme Hellinger distance}, characterizing the average-case performance of Petz recovery. To demonstrate the scope of this model, we develop partition-based constructions across diverse quantum systems and geometries, placing exact and approximate correction on equal footing. These constructions lead to a metric--error alignment hierarchy for Hilbert spaces, metrics, and error families, which in turn characterizes the resulting recovery guarantees. They yield the first known asymptotically good code families for fermionic systems, one-dimensional Rydberg-blockaded systems, and deletion errors, and extend to other physical platforms.

</details>
