**Summary.** The research analyzes time-resolved Interparticle Coulombic Decay (ICD) by coupling electronic decay theory with dissociative nuclear motion. The authors demonstrate that extracting the true decay lifetime requires careful consideration of the underlying temporal structure, as simple exponential fitting can lead to erroneous results. This provides a crucial methodological guide for interpreting ultrafast spectroscopy in molecular physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it tackles the complex interplay between electronic excitation dynamics and molecular structure (nuclear wavepacket evolution) in ultrafast processes, which is a core theme in advanced AMO physics and quantum optics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to accurately extract the true decay lifetime ($\tau$) governing time-resolved Interparticle Coulombic Decay (ICD) by correctly modeling the influence of dissociative nuclear dynamics on the measured electronic spectrum.

**Main result.** A conventional mono-exponential fit can yield a significantly different lifetime than the underlying physical value; applying a more complex fitting model yields an ICD lifetime ($\tau \approx 73$ fs) consistent with previous theoretical predictions.

**Method.** The authors developed and applied an analytical description of time-resolved electronic decay spectra, extending it to include dissociative nuclear dynamics, and compared results from mono-exponential versus double-exponential fitting models.

**Model / system.** The system is the neon dimer undergoing ICD following photoionization. The theoretical framework involves solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation with a Hamiltonian partitioned into non-decaying, coupling, and light-matter interaction terms, incorporating repulsive Coulomb potentials for the final state continuum.

**Key observables.** Time-resolved ICD electron spectrum $P(E_{\text{kin}}, E_p, t)$ and the integrated decay signal vs. time ($t$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Decay lifetime ($\tau$), internuclear distance ($R$), photoelectron energy ($E_p$), and kinetic energy of the emitted ICD electron ($E_{\text{kin}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Key approximations include assuming a product ansatz for the total state, approximating the coupling matrix element factorization, and ignoring interactions between emitted electrons in the continuum.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically illustrates energy levels and decay pathways (direct vs. resonance); Figure 2 shows the repulsive Coulomb potential and associated eigenfunctions; later figures compare experimental data fits using different exponential models.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the theoretical framework for time-resolved ICD spectra, detailing the necessary analytical extensions to include nuclear motion, presenting the results of fitting simulated/experimental data with various decay functions, and concluding with implications for general lifetime extraction techniques.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Electronic decay processes provide a fascinating window into correlated electronic rearrangements occurring on ultrafast timescales. Following these dynamics in real time has become increasingly accessible experimentally, but extracting the underlying electronic dynamics from measured spectra requires understanding how nuclear motion shapes the observable signal. Here, we extend an analytical description of time-resolved electronic decay spectra to include dissociative nuclear dynamics and apply it to Interparticle Coulombic Decay (ICD) in the neon dimer. The resulting spectra reproduce the experimentally observed spectral shape and reveal an unexpectedly important role of interference between pathways involving different vibronic resonance states. We further establish a clear connection between the temporal build-up of the spectral structure and the nuclear wavepacket dynamics in the decaying electronic state. Most strikingly, our analytical expressions reveal that the time-dependent integrated ICD signal contains contributions proportional to both $\exp(-t/τ)$ and $\exp[-t/(2τ)]$. Nevertheless, a conventional mono-exponential fit can describe the temporal signal remarkably well while yielding a decay lifetime that differs substantially from the underlying value. Applying the theoretically derived fitting model to experimental data for the neon dimer yields an ICD lifetime $τ$ of 73 fs, rather than the previously extracted 150(50) fs, placing the experimental value within the range of previous theoretical predictions. Since the underlying temporal structure is common to electronic decay processes, our findings have implications for extracting lifetimes from time-resolved decay spectra well beyond ICD.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates how uniaxial strain affects the magnetism of few-layer $	ext{CrI}_3$ by combining magnetostriction experiments on bulk crystals with theoretical calculations. The key finding is that surface effects dominate the magnetoelastic response, allowing researchers to study crucial magnetic couplings in both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases using readily available single crystals.

**Why it may be interesting.** The detailed study of magnetoelastic coupling using measurable bulk properties (magnetostriction) provides an accessible route to probe quantum magnetic phenomena typically restricted to highly controlled 2D systems or high-pressure environments, which is relevant for understanding emergent quantum states in layered materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To elucidate the role of uniaxial lattice strain on the magnetic properties and magnetoelastic coupling in few-layer $	ext{CrI}_3$ without requiring material exfoliation.

**Main result.** Magnetostriction is highly sensitive to surface effects, allowing separate investigation of in-plane and out-of-plane strain. The surface antiferromagnetic (SAFM) phase exhibits magnetostrictive responses significantly larger than those in the bulk ferromagnetic (BFM) phase.

**Method.** The study combines high-resolution magnetostriction experiments on bulk single crystals with ab-initio magnetoelastic calculations using first-principles methods.

**Model / system.** The physical system is the van der Waals semiconductor $	ext{CrI}_3$, which exhibits distinct BFM and SAFM magnetic phases. The analysis models the interplay between strain, magnetism, and surface/bulk contributions to the overall material properties.

**Key observables.** Magnetostriction ($	ext{d}L/	ext{L}$), magnetization ($M$), uniaxial strain dependence of interlayer coupling ($J^{m SAFM}_{\perp}$), and spin-flip field ($B^*$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Critical temperatures ($T_{m C}=61\,\mathrm{K}$, $T^* \simeq 50\,\mathrm{K}$), strain magnitude, and the ratio of surface to bulk contributions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The study assumes that magnetostriction measurements can effectively probe directional strain effects, overcoming historical limitations to hydrostatic pressure only.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 shows measured isothermal magnetostriction ($	ext{d}L/	ext{L}$) and corresponding magnetization ($M$) curves for both $B \parallel c$ and $B \parallel ab$.

**Paper structure.** The paper structure moves from establishing the potential of $	ext{CrI}_3$ for spintronics to presenting experimental magnetostriction data, followed by theoretical calculations that separate strain effects in the BFM and SAFM phases.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The persistence of ferromagnetic long-range order in monolayers of the van der Waals semiconductor CrI$_3$ opens new routes for spintronic applications based on two-dimensional quantum magnets. In the fabrication of such devices, the constituent materials inevitably experience anisotropic strain, which modifies their intrinsic electronic properties. At the same time, strain can serve as a powerful tuning parameter, driving the material to desired regimes. While several theoretical studies have investigated the effect of biaxial in-plane strain on CrI$_3$ numerically, experiments are widely limited to the application of hydrostatic pressure. Here, we perform high-resolution magnetostriction experiments on bulk CrI$_3$ samples, and \textit{ab-initio}-based magnetoelastic calculations, to elucidate the role of uniaxial lattice strain on the magnetic properties. Our data show that magnetostriction in CrI$_3$ is unexpectedly sensitive to surface effects, which enables us to investigate the influence of in-plane and out-of-plane strain separately, in both the bulk ferromagnetic (BFM) phase emerging at $T_{\rm C}=61\,\mathrm{K}$ and the surface antiferromagnetic (SAFM) phase below $T^* \simeq 50\,\mathrm{K}$. In particular, we quantify the uniaxial strain dependence of the surface interlayer coupling $J^{\rm SAFM}_{\perp}$ and the surface spin-flip field $B^*$, which drastically exceed the strain effects in the BFM phase by a factor of $\sim 30$. The large magnetostrictive response allows us to study the magnetoelastic coupling in few-layer CrI$_3$ through experiments on bulk single crystals, without requiring exfoliation.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces the Protocol for Optimal Cavity-Enabled Gates (POCEG) to realize high-fidelity two-qubit gates between noisy qubits coupled via an optical cavity. By applying tailored pulsed sequences, the protocol successfully mitigates fidelity loss caused by spectral detuning in both low and high damping environments. This demonstrates a pathway toward scalable quantum computation using solid-state emitters.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses a major bottleneck in solid-state quantum computing—decoherence due to spectral mismatch—by proposing engineered pulse sequences that stabilize gate operations. It bridges theoretical control techniques with practical platform limitations.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is achieving high-fidelity two-qubit gates mediated by a cavity when the constituent qubits suffer from spectral noise or significant detuning.

**Main result.** A protocol (POCEG) was developed that successfully overcomes spectral mismatches, enabling state transfer fidelities exceeding 99.9% in both low and high damping rate regimes.

**Method.** The authors employ theoretical analysis using the average Hamiltonian theory and time-dependent pulse sequences to engineer robust quantum gates.

**Model / system.** The system consists of two solid-state qubits coupled to a single optical cavity mode. The dynamics are governed by a complex Hamiltonian incorporating time-dependent couplings and detunings, analyzed via master equations.

**Key observables.** State transfer fidelity ($F$), which is the primary metric; also analyzed are cavity occupation probabilities ($n_c$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Qubit/Cavity detunings ($\Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}$), cavity damping rate ($\kappa$), and control parameters like pulse sequence length or number of pulses ($N_p$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on perturbative expansions (e.g., Magnus expansion) assuming small inter-pulse delays ($	au$) relative to other timescales, and truncating the Hilbert space based on cavity excitation levels.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate fidelity deterioration under uncontrolled evolution versus improvement using POCEG; they also map out the parameter space where high fidelity is maintained as a function of detuning and pulse number.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem, develops the POCEG protocol for both low and high damping regimes (using different control sequences), derives an effective Hamiltonian via average Hamiltonian theory, and finally simulates state transfer fidelity to demonstrate robustness against spectral noise.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

When two quantum bits are coupled through a cavity, a two-qubit gate can be realized between them either in the near-resonant regime over a timescale established by the coupling strength of the qubits with the cavity, or in the dispersive regime, over a longer timescale established by the combination of the coupling strength and the frequency detuning between the qubits and the cavity. When the qubits are spectrally noisy or differently detuned from the cavity, the fidelity for the operation can be drastically reduced in either case, precluding scalable realizations. We introduce the protocol for optimal cavity-enabled gates (POCEG) that is shown, through reliable numerical and analytical solutions, to overcome spectral differences between quantum bits and to achieve high fidelity between disparate/noisy quantum emitters. Namely, for a cavity with low damping rate, we apply a sequence of pulses to the qubits at the frequency of the cavity while periodically modulating the coupling of the qubits to the cavity. Alternatively, in the case of a large damping rate, we operate in the dispersive regime and overcome spectral disparities by applying the pulses at a frequency far-detuned from the cavity. In both instances, we find for the quantum state transfer between the two qubits that, with a modest inter-pulse delay, the fidelity that would otherwise be strongly suppressed by the spectral mismatch of the qubits can be increased beyond 99.9%. These protocols have the capacity to bring two-qubit gates between solid state systems across the threshold required for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proves that almost all pure entangled states possess the capability to share nonlocality among an arbitrary number of observers. This is achieved by linking the phenomenon to Hardy's paradox and constructing a protocol using local ancillas and projective measurements. It establishes that two-sided nonlocality sharing is a generic feature of quantum entanglement.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful demonstration of how fundamental quantum correlations (Hardy paradox) can be leveraged to establish robust, scalable nonlocality resources necessary for quantum communication protocols.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper establishes a general connection between Hardy's paradox correlations and the ability to share nonlocality among an arbitrarily large number of distant observer pairs in sequential bipartite measurements.

**Main result.** It is shown that almost all pure entangled quantum states (excluding the maximally entangled state) can facilitate two-sided nonlocality sharing using only projective measurements and a small local ancilla system.

**Method.** The authors use the CHSH inequality as a diagnostic tool, linking its violation to the existence of Hardy correlations within the shared entangled state in a sequential measurement protocol.

**Model / system.** The model involves a bipartite quantum system ($	ext{|\Psiangle_{AB}}$) distributed to two parties (Alice and Bob), who then perform sequential measurements assisted by local ancilla qubits or qutrits.

**Key observables.** CHSH value ($S$), which must exceed the classical bound of $3/4$; Hardy correlations, characterized by specific zero probabilities in correlation tables.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The entanglement structure of the state (Schmidt coefficients $\lambda_i$); measurement strategies defined by parameters like $\alpha, eta, \gamma$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The protocol assumes the availability of a local memory register/ancilla to track measurement history and that measurements are projective.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the sequential setup involving the source, entangled state, and ancillas for chains of observers; tables detail probability distributions for various measurement strategies (I, II, III).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds by first connecting Hardy's paradox to nonlocality sharing in a general bipartite setting. It then develops a protocol using an ancilla to demonstrate simultaneous CHSH violation across multiple pairs of observers, culminating in the proof that this is generic for most entangled states.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We establish a connection between Hardy's paradox and nonlocality sharing in sequential bipartite scenarios, where each subsystem is measured in turn by a chain of observers. We show that any correlations exhibiting a Hardy paradox in the two-input two-output scenario enable sequential violations of the CHSH inequality between arbitrarily many pairs of observers, using only projective measurements and the assistance of a small local ancilla system. Since almost all pure entangled states, with the only exception of the maximally entangled one, admit Hardy correlations, our protocol applies generically: almost all pure entangled states, if assisted by a local ancilla, allow for nonlocality sharing between arbitrarily many observer pairs using only projective measurements.

</details>

### [An Integrated DFT-Wannier-Quantum Embedding Pipeline for Strongly Correlated Materials: Scaling Benchmarks in Li-hBN](http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23590v1)

**Authors:** Hermawan Kresno Dipojono  
**Type:** theory · **Category:** strongly correlated electrons · **PDF:** <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.23590v1>  
**Analysis basis:** full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
**Topic relevance:** `methods for driven-dissipative` **3/5** · `Keldysh / 2PI / non-Gaussian methods` **1/5** · `analog quantum simulation` **1/5** · `driven-dissipative phase transition` **1/5**

**Summary.** The paper introduces an integrated computational pipeline combining DFT with ADAPT-VQE to simulate strongly correlated materials like Li-hBN. By using Wannier functions and advanced tensor network techniques (MPS), it overcomes the exponential memory wall associated with large active spaces. This establishes a rigorous performance baseline for future hybrid quantum-classical simulations in condensed matter physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial blueprint for applying quantum computing methods (like VQE) to condensed matter problems, specifically addressing the resource scaling issues inherent in simulating strongly correlated materials beyond current hardware limits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is developing a scalable computational method to accurately simulate strongly correlated electronic systems, which are difficult for standard DFT methods.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated an end-to-end pipeline that can process up to 28 active orbitals by employing tensor network techniques, establishing a clear performance benchmark for hybrid quantum-classical simulation.

**Method.** The approach integrates DFT calculations with the ADAPT-VQE framework, enhanced by GOCP and MPS tensor networks to manage the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space.

**Model / system.** The study uses Lithium Hexagonal Boron Nitride (Li-hBN) as a benchmark system. The electronic structure is modeled via Wannier functions derived from DFT, leading to an active-space Hamiltonian suitable for quantum embedding.

**Key observables.** Variational energies calculated by ADAPT-VQE; the relationship between active-space size and computational demand.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Active space size (benchmarked from 8 to 14 spatial orbitals); MPS bond dimension ($\chi_{\max} = 64$); singular value truncation threshold ($\epsilon_{	ext{trunc}} = 10^{-8}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary limitation addressed is the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space, necessitating the use of bounded tensor networks (MPS) for tractability.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 shows onsite energy distributions; Table 2 summarizes variational energies and scaling parameters across different qubit counts (16 to 28 qubits).

**Paper structure.** The paper outlines an end-to-end pipeline: DFT relaxation $ightarrow$ NSCF calculations $ightarrow$ Wannier localization, followed by the ADAPT-VQE simulation using GOCP and MPS tensor networks.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The seamless integration of Density Functional Theory (DFT) with quantum variational algorithms is essential for the predictive simulation of strongly correlated materials. In this work, we present an end-to-end computational pipeline - comprising DFT geometry relaxation, non-self-consistent field (NSCF) calculations, and Wannier-based orbital localization - to prepare active-space Hamiltonians for quantum embedding. We utilize the Adaptive Variational Quantum Eigensolver (ADAPT-VQE) framework, significantly enhanced by a Greedy-Operator Commutativity Partitioning (GOCP) approach and a Taylor-expanded O(5) operator evolution strategy to efficiently manage the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space. We demonstrate this framework through a systematic benchmark study of Li-hBN, mapping the system onto qubit registers and investigating the convergence behavior as the active space is expanded from 8 to 14 spatial orbitals. Our results quantify the relationship between active-space size and computational demand, identifying a critical "scaling wall" where classical simulation costs transition from manageable to intractable. This study provides a rigorous performance baseline for the DFT-to-ADAPT-VQE workflow and offers empirical insights into the memory and processing limits currently facing hybrid quantum-classical architectures using advanced co-processing strategies.

</details>

**Summary.** This work uses high-frequency Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) on $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GeTe}_2$ to characterize its magnetic anisotropy and spin dynamics. Key findings include confirming easy-axis ferromagnetism, measuring a large magnon gap, and showing that the material's magnetic properties are extremely sensitive to minor changes in chemical stoichiometry. It establishes this compound as an excellent model system for studying tunable magnetism in 2D materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study provides quantitative measurements of magnon excitations and magnetic anisotropy in a highly tunable 2D system, which is crucial for understanding emergent quantum phenomena in low-dimensional magnets relevant to spintronics and quantum simulation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To gain quantitative insights into the magnetic anisotropy and spin dynamics of quasi-two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals ferromagnets, specifically investigating the role of Fe stoichiometry.

**Main result.** The study established $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GeTe}_2$ as an easy-axis ferromagnet with a large magnon gap ($\approx 87.8 	ext{ GHz}$ at $3 	ext{ K}$) and demonstrated that spin dynamics are extremely sensitive to small variations in Fe content.

**Method.** The primary methods involved comprehensive Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) measurements across wide ranges of frequencies, temperatures, and magnetic fields, supplemented by magnetization measurements ($M-T$, $M-H$).

**Model / system.** The physical system is the near-stoichiometric van der Waals ferromagnet $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GeTe}_2$, which exhibits itinerant magnetism in a quasi-two-dimensional layered structure.

**Key observables.** Magnetic anisotropy, internal magnetic field evolution with temperature, uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy ($K_{	ext{int}}$), and the zero-field magnon gap ($\Delta$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Low temperatures (e.g., $3 	ext{ K}$), specific stoichiometry variations ($	ext{Fe}_{3.03} 	ext{GeTe}_2$), and high magnetic fields ($16 	ext{ T}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on fitting the experimental data to established models for uniaxial ferromagnets, assuming the material behaves as a model vdW ferromagnet.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate crystal structure details (hexagonal symmetry), temperature dependence of magnetization ($M-T$), and how magnetic anisotropy parameters vary with field orientation relative to the $c$-axis.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first characterizing the material's basic ferromagnetic nature via frequency-dependent ESR, then analyzing the temperature evolution of the internal field to detect short-range correlations above $T_C$, and finally quantifying anisotropy parameters like $K_{	ext{int}}$ and $\Delta$ using spin-wave analysis.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quasi-two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) ferromagnets such as the series Fe$_{3-x}$GeTe$_2$, with a relatively high Curie temperature and robust metallicity, offer an ideal platform for investigating itinerant magnetism in reduced dimensions. Here, we present a comprehensive electron spin resonance (ESR) investigation of single-crystalline almost-stoichiometric Fe$_{3.03 \pm 0.03}$GeTe$_{2}$ across wide ranges of frequencies, temperatures, and magnetic fields to gain quantitative insights into its magnetic anisotropy and spin dynamics. Frequency-dependent ESR measurements establish Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$ as an easy-axis ferromagnet. Temperature-dependent high-field ESR reveals a large internal field that gradually decreases at higher temperatures. Remarkably, this internal field persists even above $T_\mathrm{C}$, evidencing short-range spin correlations in Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$. Analysis of spin-wave modes yields a strong uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy $K_{\text{int}} \approx - 5 \times 10^6$ erg cm$^{-3}$ at 3 K and a large magnon gap $Δ(3 \mathrm{K})$ $\approx$ 87.8 $\pm$ 13.7 GHz ($\approx$ 0.363 $\pm$ 0.057 meV). Our study highlights that small variations in Fe content in Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$ lead to substantial changes in the magnon gap at low temperatures, indicating the extreme sensitivity of spin dynamics to the chemical composition. These results establish Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$ as a model vdW ferromagnet for exploring tunable anisotropies and magnon excitations in metallic 2D magnets.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops an enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Network scheme (PINNQOC) for solving quantum optimal control problems. It benchmarks this ML approach against established methods like Krotov's and PRONTO's on multi-level qubit systems. The results show that PINNQOC achieves high fidelity while offering a promising pathway for real-time, adaptive control in future autonomous quantum hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the practical implementation challenges in quantum computing by providing a machine learning approach (PINN) that can automate pulse engineering and adapt to hardware imperfections better than purely analytical or trajectory-dependent solvers.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is achieving high-fidelity quantum gate operations while actively suppressing population leakage into non-computational states.

**Main result.** The proposed PINNQOC framework successfully matches the fidelity of traditional solvers (Krotov, PRONTO) and demonstrates superior leakage suppression in multi-level systems.

**Method.** The authors propose an enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Network scheme (PINNQOC) to solve quantum optimal control problems, benchmarking it against established gradient-based methods like Krotov's and PRONTO's optimization techniques.

**Model / system.** The study uses truncated multi-level systems as models, specifically a three-level fluxonium qubit and a four-level Nitrogen-Vacancy center coupled to a Carbon-13 nuclear spin. The dynamics are governed by the time-dependent Schrödinger equation.

**Key observables.** Gate fidelity (target vs. achieved), mean population leakage ($\ell$), computational time, and iteration efficiency.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Penalization factors ($q=0.2$ or $0.3$), target gate specifications, and the number of time steps ($N_t$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Standard PINNs suffer from numerical bottlenecks (spectral bias) when solving highly oscillatory dynamics; traditional solvers are strictly trajectory-specific.

**Figures summary.** The notes indicate comparisons across multiple tables summarizing performance metrics for different gate types and system sizes, comparing fidelity, leakage, time, and iterations for the three methods.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of high-fidelity control, details the theoretical background of QOC (Krotov/PRONTO), presents the novel PINNQOC framework enhancements, benchmarks performance on specific multi-level qubits, and concludes with an analysis of computational trade-offs for autonomous quantum hardware.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Achieving scalable quantum computing demands high-fidelity operations capable of mitigating population leakage into non-computational states. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm to unify quantum hardware characterization (inverse problems) and pulse engineering (direct problems), laying the foundational architecture for autonomous quantum processors. However, standard PINN frameworks face severe numerical bottlenecks, such as spectral bias, when attempting to simultaneously solve highly oscillatory multi-level dynamics and optimize continuous control fields under strict global phase constraints. In this work, we propose an enhanced PINN scheme for quantum optimal control (PINNQOC) that circumvents these limitations by incorporating Fourier feature embeddings, dynamic epoch normalization, and an informed pre-training routine. To rigorously evaluate its performance, we systematically benchmark our framework against two premier continuous control solvers: the first-order Krotov method and the second-order Projection Operator Newton Method for Trajectory Optimization (PRONTO). These techniques are applied to implement multiple quantum gates on a truncated three-level fluxonium qubit and a four-level Nitrogen-Vacancy center coupled to a Carbon-13 nuclear spin. Our advanced PINNQOC approach successfully suppresses population leakage while achieving gate fidelities exceeding 99.9$\%$, matching the efficacy of traditional solvers. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of computational times, iteration efficiency, and mean leakage, highlighting the distinct trade-offs and avenues for embedding physics-guided machine learning into automated quantum hardware pipelines.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes a novel 'fully-quantum Metropolis walk' algorithm designed to sample complex probability distributions arising from Ising models. By making both proposal and acceptance steps inherently quantum via Hamiltonian simulation, the authors achieve significant theoretical speedups over existing quantum walk methods. This work establishes that super-quadratic advantages are achievable for sampling problems in condensed matter physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses how advanced quantum walk techniques can provide polynomial speedups for sampling problems relevant to spin glasses and disordered systems, pushing beyond previously assumed quadratic limits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is efficiently sampling from the low-temperature Gibbs distribution of classical dense Ising models, which is a key problem in statistical physics.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that fully-quantum Metropolis walks can achieve an asymptotic advantage of about a cubic polynomial over previous quantum walk methods, suggesting super-quadratic speedups are possible.

**Method.** They introduce 'fully-quantum Metropolis walks' where both proposal and acceptance steps are intrinsically quantum, utilizing Hamiltonian simulation for the proposal mechanism within a Szegedy quantum walk framework.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on classical dense Ising models defined by a Hamiltonian $H(\mathbf{x})$, aiming to sample the low-temperature Gibbs distribution $\pi_eta(x)$. The analysis involves simulating annealing paths across various inverse temperatures ($eta$).

**Key observables.** Total variation distance ($\|q - \pi_eta\|_{TV}$), spectral gap ($\delta_eta$), and query complexity (classical vs. quantum counts).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Inverse temperature $eta$, error tolerance $\epsilon$, system size $n$, and the annealing schedule parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on fault-tolerant compilation of primitives, using a Zeno-rewind protocol to manage spectral projections, and assuming parallel execution for Pauli measurements.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare resource requirements (e.g., surface code distance vs. $n$) across different proposals (local, uniform, Hamiltonian) and varying error tolerances ($\epsilon$), showing the crossover point where quantum walks outperform classical methods.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the sampling problem using MCMC/quantum walks to introducing the novel fully-quantum proposal mechanism. It then details the resource scaling analysis across an annealing schedule, culminating in runtime comparisons against state-of-the-art classical and quantum approaches.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We introduce a new class of fully-quantum Metropolis walks in which both the proposal and acceptance steps are intrinsically quantum. Unlike standard quantum walks obtained by quantizing classically efficient Markov chains, our algorithm employs Hamiltonian simulation as a quantum-native proposal mechanism, enlarging the class of quantum walks beyond classical counterparts. We target the problem of sampling from the low-temperature Gibbs distribution of classical dense Ising models, within a fixed error in total variation distance. This approach achieves about a cubic polynomial asymptotic advantage over previous quantum-walks, resulting in a total sixth-degree polynomial queries speedup compared to the best classical walk. This shows that speedups beyond the widely assumed quadratic limit are possible within the quantum walk formalism. We perform a complete fault-tolerant compilation of all algorithmic primitives and benchmark against CPU, GPU, and FPGA implementations of the best classical Markov chain. Under identical hardware assumptions, the resulting advantage runtime crossover is reduced from approximately $10^3$ years for conventional quantum walks to less than one day. These results identify fully-quantum Markov chains as a promising route toward practical quantum advantage.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a quantum-enhanced technique for estimating channel impairments like dispersion and delay in low-photon-number optical links. By employing a Quantum Pulse Gate with photon-number resolution, the authors show that they can achieve measurement precision limited only by fundamental quantum noise, surpassing classical bounds.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly applies advanced quantum information techniques (QFI, POVMs) to a practical problem in quantum communication (optical fiber links), providing concrete bounds on achievable sensing precision below the SQL.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is establishing the quantum limit for blind joint estimation of group delay ($	au$) and second-order dispersion ($\kappa$) in photon-starved coherent optical links.

**Main result.** A Quantum Pulse Gate (QPG) combined with Photon-Number-Resolving Detectors (PNRDs) measurement locally attains the Quantum Cramér–Rao Bound, achieving performance below the Standard Quantum Limit (SQL).

**Method.** The analysis uses quantum estimation theory, deriving the effective Quantum Fisher Information matrix by exploiting parity decomposition and eliminating unknown common carrier phases via a Schur complement.

**Model / system.** The system models coherent state discrimination in fiber links suffering from residual dispersion. The measurement setup involves projecting the field onto phase-diverse temporal modes using a QPG followed by PNRD detection.

**Key observables.** Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrix, error probabilities ($P_e$), and the covariance matrix $C$ of centered generators.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Average photon number ($N_s$), residual dispersion ($\kappa$), group delay ($	au$), and detector efficiency ($\eta_d$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis neglects third-order dispersion, assumes equiprobable M-ary PSK states, and utilizes the Schur complement to eliminate unknown common phase dependence.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the proposed temporal-mode-assisted receiver setup and compare error probabilities for different mode-recovery strategies under simulated residual dispersion, showing performance below the SQL.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the physical problem (dispersion in coherent links) to deriving the QCRB using quantum measurement theory. It details the construction of the optimal QPG/PNRD measurement and concludes by demonstrating that this method surpasses classical limits for blind parameter estimation.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Residual dispersion breaks temporal-mode matching in photon-starved coherent links. For equiprobable $M$-ary PSK coherent states in a known spectral mode, with unknown symbols and carrier phase, we establish the quantum limit for blind joint estimation of group delay and second-order dispersion: after eliminating the common phase, it is $4N_s\mathbf{C}$, set by the covariance of the centered generators alone. A multi-output quantum pulse gate with photon-number-resolving detection locally attains it and supports reception below the standard quantum limit under turbulent fading.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper evaluates Quantum Krylov Diagonalization (QKD) as a method to find ground-state energies of the 1D Hubbard model. It systematically analyzes how algorithmic choices—such as evolution time and basis truncation—affect convergence and stability. The results confirm that QKD is a viable, hardware-efficient tool for studying strongly correlated fermionic systems on current quantum processors.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides concrete, actionable guidelines for applying advanced quantum algorithms (QKD) to benchmark strongly correlated models like the Hubbard model on near-term noisy hardware, bridging theory with experimental feasibility.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Estimating ground-state properties of strongly correlated quantum systems, which is computationally intractable due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space.

**Main result.** Quantum Krylov Diagonalization (QKD) proves to be a practical and hardware-efficient method for studying these systems on current NISQ processors, provided algorithmic parameters are carefully balanced.

**Method.** The study uses QKD, a hybrid quantum-classical approach, to estimate extremal eigenvalues by constructing and diagonalizing a projected Hamiltonian matrix derived from time evolution simulations.

**Model / system.** The primary model is the one-dimensional (1D) Hubbard model with periodic boundary conditions. The system's dynamics are mapped onto qubits using the Jordan–Wigner transformation, resulting in a Hamiltonian expressed as a sum of Pauli strings.

**Key observables.** Ground State Energy (GSE), spectral gap $\Delta(s)$, and the absolute GSE error ($\Delta E$) monitored against the Krylov dimension ($D$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Krylov dimension, time-evolution parameter ($	ext{tevol}$), Trotter number ($N_{	ext{trot}}$), Singular-Value Truncation (SVT) threshold, and interaction strength ($U_0$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on approximating the time evolution operator via first-order Trotterization and requires regularization (SVD) to handle near linear dependencies in the basis states.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the 1D Hubbard chain setup, quantum circuits for time evolution, convergence of GSE error vs. Krylov dimension/Trotter steps, and spectral gap analysis along interpolation paths.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically investigates QKD performance by analyzing its dependence on various algorithmic parameters (Krylov dimension, Trotterization) using the 1D Hubbard model. It details the mathematical framework for constructing projected matrices ($	ilde{H}, 	ilde{S}$) and validates the approach both through ideal simulations and actual measurements on IBM quantum hardware.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum Krylov diagonalization (QKD) has emerged as a promising hybrid quantum-classical approach for estimating ground-state properties of many-body systems on near-term quantum devices. In this work, we investigate the convergence, stability, and hardware performance of QKD for the one-dimensional Hubbard model with periodic boundary conditions. Building upon our previously developed low-depth Jordan--Wigner implementation, which reduces the number of two-qubit (CNOT) gates required for quantum time evolution, we perform a systematic study of the influence of the Krylov dimension, Hamiltonian evolution parameters, system size, interaction strength, and singular-value truncation (SVT) on the convergence of the method. Our results show that the performance of QKD is governed by a delicate interplay between the low-energy spectral structure of the Hamiltonian and numerical stability. In particular, systems with near-closing energy gaps require longer evolution times to efficiently resolve nearby eigenstates, while the evolution time, Krylov dimension, Trotter number, and SVT threshold must be carefully balanced to avoid numerical instabilities and accumulated time-discretization errors. This analysis provides practical guidelines for selecting algorithmic parameters in QKD. Finally, we demonstrate the algorithm on IBM quantum hardware, where the experimental results reproduce the convergence trends predicted by ideal simulations using only lightweight readout-error mitigation and a modest measurement budget. Together, these results demonstrate that QKD is a practical and hardware-efficient approach for studying strongly correlated fermionic systems on current NISQ quantum processors.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes the security of Bitcoin against two competing quantum miners by developing a game-theoretic model. By calculating optimal strategies that allow for multiple measurements, the authors demonstrate that these advanced quantum mining techniques do not significantly lower the network's 51% attack threshold in practice. The work is crucial for assessing future quantum threats to Proof-of-Work cryptocurrencies.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly focused on AMO physics, the rigorous application of quantum computation concepts (like Grover's algorithm and measurement uncertainty) within a complex, real-world decentralized system provides an excellent case study for modeling open quantum systems under adversarial conditions.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To study how two quantum-enabled Bitcoin miners affect the network's 51% attack threshold when playing a competitive game against each other.

**Main result.** The optimal quantum mining strategies, even those incorporating aggressive measurements, have a negligible effect on the established 51% attack threshold of the Bitcoin network under current difficulty regimes.

**Method.** The authors extended existing game-theoretic frameworks by computing payoff matrices and determining Nash equilibria for two non-colluding miners. They simulated these optimal strategies within the classical Bitcoin protocol structure.

**Model / system.** The model is an otherwise classical Bitcoin network infiltrated by two aggressive quantum miners (Alice and Bob). The analysis incorporates concepts like UTXOs, SHA-256 hashing, and extends game theory to include multiple quantum measurements between block attempts.

**Key observables.** The resulting threshold for the 51% attack; stale rate ($	ext{pstale}$); detection probability ($	ext{Pdet}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Network difficulty ($D$); number of Grover iterations ($\kappa$); number of measurements ($c$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the miners employ optimal strategies derived from game theory and accounts for multiple measurement opportunities, unlike prior single-computation models.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the structure of a Bitcoin block header and show simulated metrics like $	ext{P95}$ and $	ext{Pdet}$ as functions of network difficulty ($D$).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the classical Bitcoin cryptographic model (transactions, UTXOs) to setting up a game-theoretic framework using payoff matrices for quantum mining strategies. The core analysis then simulates these optimal strategies across different difficulty regimes.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the impact that two miners equipped with quantum computers purpose-built for quantum Bitcoin mining will have on the 51% attack threshold of the Bitcoin network, given that the miners are playing a competitive game against each other to be the first to mine a block. We extend an existing game-theoretic framework for Bitcoin mining and compute the resultant payoff matrices. From these payoff matrices, we determine optimal quantum mining strategies for two non-colluding and aggressive quantum miners with multiple opportunities at finding a valid block in an otherwise classical Bitcoin network. We show that these optimal quantum mining strategies have a negligible effect on the 51% attack threshold. The novelty of our work is the inclusion of the Aggressive Quantum Mining Strategy and the realistic approach of allowing the quantum miners to restart their search if their measurements do not yield a valid block when determining the optimal quantum mining strategies. Our result is important for evaluating quantum-mining threats on cryptocurrencies based on Proof-of-Work, e.g. Bitcoin

</details>

**Summary.** This paper establishes the 2D Uhlenbeck-Ford model as a robust and highly accurate reference fluid for calculating the thermodynamic properties of other two-dimensional fluids. By combining exact virial expansions with advanced free-energy techniques like Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamic Integration, the authors validate its use across various physical regimes.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical fluids, the rigorous application of advanced statistical mechanics techniques like NETI for free-energy calculations provides methodological insights applicable to determining equilibrium properties in complex quantum many-body systems where direct simulation is hard.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates using the Uhlenbeck-Ford (UF) model as a highly accurate reference system for calculating the free energy of two-dimensional (2D) fluids.

**Main result.** The 2D UF model was shown to be an excellent reference fluid, accurately predicting thermodynamic properties and remaining thermodynamically stable in the fluid phase up to significant scaling parameters ($p \lesssim 70$).

**Method.** The authors employed advanced statistical mechanics techniques including exact computation of virial coefficients (up to tenth order) and Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamic Integration (NETI).

**Model / system.** The system analyzed is the 2D Uhlenbeck-Ford (UF) model, characterized by a specific pair potential. The methodology involves constructing an equation of state and excess Helmholtz free energy using this reference fluid.

**Key observables.** Equation of State (EOS), excess Helmholtz free energy ($eta F_{exc}$), phase diagram boundaries, reduced pressure ($eta b P$), and structural order parameters ($\Psi_6$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Dimensionless density variable ($x$) and the scaling parameter $p$, which dictates stability limits.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary approximations involve truncating the virial expansion (up to 10th order) and using NETI, whose errors are related to finite switching times.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares reduced pressure vs. dimensionless variable $x$ for the 2D UF model, contrasting exact virial expansions with Molecular Dynamics simulation data.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the accuracy of the UF model via high-order virial coefficient calculations and comparison to MD simulations. It then uses this reference system in thermodynamic integration methods (NETI) to calculate the free energy of a target fluid, validating its applicability against other theoretical models.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the Uhlenbeck-Ford (UF) model as a reference system for free-energy calculations in two-dimensional (2D) fluids. The 2D virial coefficients are computed exactly up to tenth order and combined with molecular simulation data to construct highly accurate numerical representations of the equation of state and the excess Helmholtz free energy. We then determine the phase diagram of the model in order to establish the thermodynamic stability limits of the fluid phase and thereby identify the range of applicability of the UF model as a fluid reference system. In the course of this analysis, we identify the solid, hexatic, and fluid phases, and show that the fluid remains the only thermodynamically stable phase, independent of density, for scaling parameters up to $p\lesssim 70$. Finally, we demonstrate the practical applicability of the 2D UF model as a reference system through thermodynamic integration calculations of the free energy of a two-dimensional Lennard-Jones fluid.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors determine the two-copy distillability threshold for Werner states using a novel and strong partial trace inequality. They prove that $\varrho(4, -1/2)$ is undistillable and establish that this state family's one-copy and two-copy distillability regions coincide when $\alpha \ge -1/2$. This advances the understanding of entanglement measures in quantum information theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, quantitative tool—the partial trace inequality—to characterize fundamental properties (like distillability) of quantum states, which has implications across quantum information theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the open question of determining the two-copy distillability of Werner states, specifically focusing on $\varrho(4, -1/2)$.

**Main result.** They prove that $\varrho(4, -1/2)$ is not two-copy distillable and establish a general criterion: $\varrho(d, \alpha)$ is undistillable if and only if $\alpha \ge -1/2$.

**Method.** The core method involves proving a strong partial trace inequality for matrices of low rank, which serves as a necessary condition for two-copy distillability.

**Model / system.** The analysis centers on the Werner state $\varrho(d, \alpha) = (I + \alpha F) / (d^2 + \alpha d)$, which is a bipartite quantum state acting on two $d$-dimensional systems.

**Key observables.** Two-copy distillability, partial trace norms ($\lVert 	ext{tr}_1(C) Vert_F$, $\lVert 	ext{tr}_2(C) Vert_F$), and the Frobenius norm of the matrix $C$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension $d$ of the subsystems, the parameter $\alpha$ defining the state, and the rank $r$ of the matrix $C$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The results rely on proving a specific partial trace inequality for matrices whose rank is bounded by $r$, utilizing advanced linear algebra techniques like balanced decomposition.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the general rank-constrained partial-trace inequality (Theorem A) using matrix decompositions, which then allows them to apply a known criterion to settle Problem 5 regarding $\varrho(4, -1/2)$ and generalize the result for all Werner states.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Problem 5 in {\it Five Open Problems in Quantum Information Theory} [PRX Quantum 3, 010101 (2022)], asks whether the two-ququart Werner state $\varrho(4,-\tfrac12)$ is two-copy distillable, where $\varrho(d,α)=(I+αF)/(d^2+αd)$. We answer it in the negative. To this end, we show the following stronger statement: for all $C\in M_{d_1d_2}(\mathbb{C})$ of rank at most $r \le d_1 d_2$, $\mathrm{tr}_1(C)\|_F^2+\|\mathrm{tr}_2(C)\|_F^2 \le r\|C\|_F^2+\frac{1}{r}|\mathrm{tr}(C)|^2$. A result by Costa Rico on the equivalence of this inequality with two-copy undistillability at $r = 2$ then settles Problem 5: $\varrho(4,-\tfrac{1}{2})$ is not two-copy distillable. Furthermore, we show that $\varrho(d,α)$ is two-copy undistillable for every $d\ge2$, if and only if $α\ge-\tfrac{1}{2}$. Thus, the one and two-copy distillability regions of $\varrho(d,α)$ coincide. These results have been found and written up with AI tools, pointing towards a structural change affecting the field of quantum information and computation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper redefines the understanding of ultimate precision in quantum sensors by linking metrological bounds to fundamental quantum speed limits. It resolves apparent paradoxes in scaling laws—such as super-Heisenberg improvements—by providing a physically grounded resource accounting method. The framework successfully reconciles different scaling regimes using dynamical constraints derived from atomic/optical models.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it provides a rigorous theoretical framework connecting quantum dynamics (speed limits) directly to achievable measurement precision in atomic/optical systems, which is central to modern AMO research.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to clarify the true scaling of precision limits (Heisenberg limit) in quantum metrology by grounding the analysis in physically derived resource accounting using quantum speed limits.

**Main result.** It shows that the Heisenberg limit is an information-theoretic manifestation of the quantum speed limit, and super-resolving protocols can be reconciled by identifying the generator norm as the relevant operational resource.

**Method.** The authors employ quantum speed limits (QSL) and relate metrological sensitivity to the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), analyzing scaling laws for phase and time estimation in specific physical models.

**Model / system.** The analysis uses general quantum sensing protocols, focusing on a concrete example of Rabi oscillations in two-level atoms driven by an $m$-photon resonance. The dynamics are governed by Hamiltonians involving photon number operators ($a^\dagger^2 a^2$).

**Key observables.** Phase error ($\delta\varphi$), time error ($\delta t$), Quantum Fisher Information ($F_Q(t)$), and the expectation value of an observable $P$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Average photon number ($n$), resonance order ($m$), and coupling constants ($\lambda$). Scaling regimes include $\delta\varphi \propto n^{-m/2}$ and $\delta\varphi \propto 1/n$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on recasting metrological bounds through dynamical speed limits, assuming ideal coherent evolution for the derivation of fundamental scaling laws.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares probability distributions ($p_{b n}(t)$) for different multiphoton coupling orders ($m=1$ vs $m=4$) in Rabi oscillations, illustrating faster dynamics for larger $m$.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem by contrasting apparent super-Heisenberg scaling with fundamental bounds. It then develops a framework using QSL and QFI to derive operational bounds, applying this to specific multiphoton resonance models before concluding on the resource identification.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum metrology promises sensitivity beyond classical strategies, yet it remains unsettled how quantum-enabled precision should scale with physical resources and how to interpret quantum advantage. We provide a physically grounded resource accounting that clarifies the true Heisenberg limit and resolves apparent super-Heisenberg paradoxes. We demonstrate that the Heisenberg limit is best viewed as an information-theoretic manifestation of the quantum speed limit. We illustrate these ideas with a simple, super-resolving phase-estimation protocol based on Rabi oscillations in two-level atoms driven on an $m$-photon resonance. In this setting, the phase error scales as $n^{-m/2}$, where $n$ is the average photon number. Recasting metrological sensitivity through quantum dynamical speed limits yields operational bounds that reconcile such super-resolution strategies with the standard Heisenberg interpretation and identify the relevant resources in the norm of the generator. We also revisit the common attribution of the NOON state's $1/n$ scaling to quantum entanglement. We show that such an attribution is not generic and the Heisenberg $1/n$ scaling does not, by itself, certify entanglement as the enabling resource.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces the Nested Integral Generator Theorem, a rigorous mathematical framework to convert operator equalities into multi-fold exact integral identities. By systematically using resolutions of the identity, it provides universal tools to calculate matrix elements for complex systems in continuous-variable quantum optics, such as those involving squeezing and nonlinear Kerr interactions.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a powerful, systematic tool that replaces potentially intractable direct calculation or approximation methods (like Trotter expansions) with exact integral formulas for complex quantum optical processes.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To establish a rigorous, representation-independent mathematical framework for calculating complex operator compositions by systematically converting them into exact multi-fold integral identities.

**Main result.** The Nested Integral Generator Theorem provides an exact $N$-fold nested integral representation for matrix elements involving chains of operators, applicable to various quantum systems.

**Method.** The core method involves starting from operator tautologies and iteratively inserting continuous resolutions of the identity, utilizing vector-valued integration theory to rigorously justify the interchange of inner products with Bochner integrals.

**Model / system.** The framework is applied to continuous-variable bosonic systems, including single-mode operators, two-mode Gaussian unitaries (squeezing, beam splitting), and nonlinear interactions like the Kerr effect. It provides exact calculations for matrix elements $\langle n| \mathcal{O} | \alpha, \lambda angle$.

**Key observables.** Exact integral representations of operator functions, such as the overlap between a Kerr-squeezed coherent state and Fock states, and two-mode Gaussian network matrix elements.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Squeezing parameters ($\zeta$), beam-splitter angles ($\varphi$), Kerr nonlinearity strength ($\chi$), and photon number ($n, m$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions involve the existence of a continuous resolution of the identity and meeting verifiable sufficient conditions (Bochner integrability) to interchange integration and projection operators.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in detail, but the notes reference specific equations (e.g., Eq. 18 for path integral analogy, Eq. 48 for compound network result, Eq. 53 for Kerr overlap).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from general operator tautologies to the Nested Integral Generator Theorem (Theorem 1), providing specific applications to Gaussian unitaries and nonlinear systems, culminating in explicit matrix element calculations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Inserting resolutions of the identity is a standard technique for representing states and operators throughout quantum theory, quantum field theory, and related areas of mathematical physics. This paper elevates this procedure to a rigorous, representation-independent framework through the Nested Integral Generator Theorem. Starting from operator tautologies, the theorem systematically generates exact multi-fold integral identities by successive insertions of continuous resolutions of the identity followed by projection onto arbitrary orthonormal basis vectors. The resulting construction applies to arbitrary finite compositions of closed operators acting on arbitrary target states and establishes a general mapping from operator equalities to families of exact integral identities. Using the theory of vector-valued integration, explicit and verifiable sufficient conditions are derived under which inner products may be interchanged rigorously with Bochner integrals, thereby placing a step that is often left implicit in the physics literature on a firm mathematical foundation. As an immediate consequence, the theorem yields exact integral representations for individual operator functions. Its scope is illustrated through elementary, polynomial, and analytic single-mode operators, as well as single- and two-mode Gaussian unitaries, including squeezing and beam splitting. The framework is further applied to two nontrivial examples beyond standard Gaussian calculations: an exact integral representation of a Kerr-squeezed coherent-state overlap and exact Fock-basis matrix elements for a composite two-mode Gaussian network expressed in terms of bivariate Hermite polynomials.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops Interval Algebraic Quantum Field Theory (IAQFT) by replacing exact mathematical states with 'quantum parcels,' which represent finite-precision information from local measurements. It successfully reformulates core concepts of relativistic quantum theory—such as modular structure and vacuum correlations—within this operational, finite-precision framework. This provides a unified theoretical tool for modeling QFT under realistic measurement constraints.

**Why it may be interesting.** For a theoretical physicist working on open quantum systems or many-body dynamics, IAQFT offers a formal way to incorporate inherent measurement limitations and computational constraints directly into the fundamental structure of QFT, moving beyond idealized continuous mathematics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is extending Algebraic Quantum Field Theory (AQFT) from exact mathematical descriptions to a rigorous framework capable of handling finite-precision information derived from physical measurements.

**Main result.** The authors introduce Interval AQFT (IAQFT), which successfully recasts major structural features of relativistic quantum theory—including modular theory and the Unruh effect—into terms involving 'quantum parcels' that encode finite precision.

**Method.** The methodology involves replacing exact states with weak* open convex regions called 'quantum parcels,' developing procedures for parcel reduction, and establishing connections between these operational objects and deep mathematical structures of operator algebras.

**Model / system.** The theory applies to relativistic quantum field theory, formulated using the algebraic approach (AQFT) based on a net of local $C^*$-algebras indexed by spacetime regions. The core mathematical machinery involves analyzing state spaces under the weak* topology.

**Key observables.** Spacelike vacuum correlations, Bell violations, and structural properties like the Reeh–Schlieder property are key diagnostics that must persist under finite precision.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The framework is defined by the geometry of quantum parcels (weak* open convex regions) and their evolution via measurement updates or refinement processes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theory assumes that exact states remain as indispensable ideal limits, recovered only through increasingly refined sequences of finite-precision parcels. The structure relies heavily on the weak* topology and its finite determination property.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds by first defining quantum parcels to replace exact states in AQFT. It then develops operational procedures like parcel reduction and measurement updates, showing how these preserve key physical features (like vacuum correlations). Finally, it connects this finite-precision framework to deep mathematical results concerning the classification of von Neumann factors.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Recent work introduced Interval Quantum Mechanics (IQM), a finite-precision framework in which physical information is represented by sets of possible states rather than exact states. We extend this approach to algebraic quantum field theory (AQFT) by introducing Interval Algebraic Quantum Field Theory (IAQFT), whose basic objects are quantum parcels: weak* open convex regions of state space encoding finite-precision information obtained from finitely many local observations.   We develop parcel reduction and measurement update, establish finite-dimensional information-contraction results, and formulate locality through compatible parcel nets. Major structural features of AQFT are recast in parcel-theoretic terms, including the Reeh--Schlieder property, Haag's theorem, modular theory, the KMS condition, and the Unruh effect. We show that spacelike vacuum correlations and strict Bell violations persist under finite precision, and that lattice approximations are compatible with the parcel framework. Finally, we recover the Murray--von Neumann classification of factors together with the trace and projection equivalence in Type~$\mathrm{II}_1$ factors from the geometry of limiting parcels. IAQFT thus provides a unified finite-precision formulation of the operational, modular, and operator-algebraic structures of relativistic quantum theory.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a comprehensive theory for optimally cooling multiple qubits by treating the system as a single closed unit. It proves that a global unitary transformation achieves the lowest possible target temperature, outperforming parallel cooling strategies. The methodology involves spectral analysis and combinatorial constraints to determine when simpler, permutation-based protocols can match this theoretical optimum.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous theoretical tools to analyze resource optimization in quantum thermodynamics, specifically quantifying how collective coupling (global unitary) improves energy extraction compared to independent local operations, which is highly relevant for designing efficient quantum refrigerators or thermalization protocols.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the closed-system problem of optimally cooling $M$ target qubits selected from a larger pool of $N$ identical thermal qubits to achieve the lowest common local temperature allowed by unitarity.

**Main result.** A universal optimal protocol exists that achieves the minimum possible mean target energy, and this global strategy strictly outperforms parallel single-target cooling methods. The analysis also provides exact criteria for when simpler permutation-only protocols suffice.

**Method.** The authors combine spectral analysis of the initial state with optimization techniques to derive an optimal unitary transformation ($U_*$) composed of a passive rearrangement and a complex-Hadamard correction. They use graph theory concepts (hypergraph coloring) to analyze feasibility conditions for permutations.

**Model / system.** The system consists of $N$ identical, noninteracting qubits initially prepared in a Gibbs state $ho(eta)$. The cooling process is modeled as the evolution under a global unitary transformation acting on this register.

**Key observables.** Local target temperature, mean target energy ($p_\star(P_1)$), and the cooling curve depth ($\xi_M^\star$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** $N$ (total qubits), $M$ (target qubits), initial inverse temperature $eta$, and the ratio of global vs. parallel cooling performance.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the system remains closed, and while a complex-Hadamard correction is optimal, alternative permutation realizations are analyzed for implementation simplicity.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate dynamic cooling protocols using global unitaries on $N$ qubits to cool $M$ targets; they also show resource allocation diagrams comparing global vs. parallel target populations for specific $(N, M)$ pairs.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the optimal protocol via two steps (passive rearrangement and Hadamard correction). It then derives necessary and sufficient arithmetic criteria for achieving this optimum using only permutations, classifying feasibility islands. Finally, it provides quantitative bounds on the achievable cooling depth by comparing global vs. parallel strategies.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We solve the closed-system problem of cooling $M$ qubits, selected from $N$ identical thermal qubits, to the lowest common local temperature allowed by unitarity. The optimal protocol consists of two conceptually distinct steps. First, a passive rearrangement assigns the largest eigenvalues of the initial state to target sectors of lowest Hamming weight, thereby minimizing the total target energy. Second, a target-only complex-Hadamard transformation within each fixed-Hamming-weight subspace equalizes the one-qubit target marginals without changing any target-sector probability or the total energy. Consequently, imposing a common local temperature costs neither cooling depth nor additional work: the constrained optimum coincides with the unconstrained passive minimum for every $N>M$ and every initial temperature. The complex-Hadamard correction may nevertheless be costly at the circuit level. We therefore derive an exact arithmetic criterion for when the same optimum can be attained by a temperature-independent computational-basis permutation alone, and exhaustively classify the resulting finite-size islands of feasibility for $M+2\leq N\leq 128$. At isolated temperatures, further optimal permutations can arise through numerical cancellations between different thermal eigenvalue shells. These alternative realizations may reduce implementation complexity, but they cannot improve the cooling curve already attained by the universal protocol. We also derive the exact cooling curve, prove that at least two ancillary qubits are necessary and sufficient for nontrivial cooling, and show that joint many-target cooling can strictly outperform parallel single-target strategies.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents a novel, unitary scheme to implement bias-preserving CNOT and Toffoli gates on cat qubits. By leveraging vacuum-conditional interactions mediated by cross-Kerr nonlinearities, the authors overcome limitations associated with dissipation-based gate schemes. This breakthrough enables fault-tolerant quantum computation by maintaining exponential suppression of bit-flip errors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it tackles fundamental resource limitations in superconducting quantum computing platforms by providing a theoretically robust method for implementing multi-qubit gates while maintaining crucial noise protection mechanisms.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is implementing logical quantum gates, specifically CNOT and Toffoli, on cat qubits while preserving the inherent exponential suppression of bit-flip errors (noise bias). Existing methods often rely on engineered dissipation, which introduces limitations.

**Main result.** The authors propose a unitary, vacuum-conditional gate scheme that successfully preserves the noise bias for both CNOT and extends it to a universal Toffoli gate. This allows for logical memory with error rates below $10^{-6}$ using repetition codes.

**Method.** The gates are realized using controlled interactions involving cross-Kerr nonlinearities ($\chi$) and beam-splitter drives ($g$). Error suppression is achieved through echo sequences (e.g., displacement echoes) to mitigate coherent phase-flip errors.

**Model / system.** The system utilizes cat qubits, which are stabilized by engineered two-photon loss. The gate mechanism involves coupling the control, target, and an auxiliary 'bin' mode via these nonlinear interactions.

**Key observables.** Bit-flip error probabilities ($p_X$) and phase-flip error probabilities ($p_Z$); logical error rates ($	ext{error} < 10^{-6}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Cat size parameter $|\alpha|^2$, interaction strengths ($\chi, g$), and the coherence time $T_1 = 1 	ext{ ms}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Assumes good component lifetimes and precise nonlinearity engineering; the gate speed is limited by coupling strengths rather than dissipation rates.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the Bloch sphere representation of X gates, the schematic setup using cross-Kerr/beam-splitter interactions for CNOT, and phase-space diagrams detailing echo sequences used for error suppression.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the bias problem in cat qubits. It details the unitary CNOT gate mechanism (Chunk 1), followed by a rigorous analysis of error channels using echo techniques (Chunk 2). Finally, it extends this methodology to implement the universal Toffoli ($	ext{CCX}$) gate (Chunk 3).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Cat qubits can exhibit strong noise bias due to their exponentially enhanced bit-flip times and only polynomially reduced phase-flip times with increasing photon number, which makes them attractive candidates for hardware-efficient quantum error correction. However, it is difficult to maintain this strong noise bias in logical operations such as CNOT gates between cats. Here, we propose a coherent CNOT gate scheme between two dissipative cats that preserves the exponential noise bias. The proposed gate relies only on unitary operations, which avoids the non-idealities associated with many existing gate schemes that rely on engineered dissipations. Assuming good component lifetimes and precise nonlinearity engineering, the proposed gate can enable logical memory in the megaquop regime (logical error rates < 10^-6) with a distance-7 repetition code consisting of 13 cat qubits.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a novel probabilistic framework to simulate multi-state discrete-time quantum walks. By mapping the quantum evolution onto classical stochastic processes driven by Poisson variables, the authors rigorously prove that these walks converge in the continuum limit to solutions of coupled Dirac partial differential equations. This offers a scalable theoretical alternative for analyzing complex quantum dynamics using classical methods.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, non-unitary classical tool (stochastic processes) to analyze complex quantum dynamics, offering potential computational advantages for simulating higher-dimensional or multi-state quantum systems where direct unitary simulation is hard.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is constructing a rigorous probabilistic representation for multi-state discrete-time quantum walks (QWs) on lattices.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrate that this classical stochastic process converges to the continuum solution of coupled linear Dirac partial differential equations in the limit.

**Method.** They derive the probabilistic formulation by mapping the unitary quantum evolution onto a system driven by independent Poisson random variables, followed by a continuous rescaling limit.

**Model / system.** The model is a multi-state discrete-time Quantum Walk on an integer lattice, generalized from two to three states using Gell-Mann matrices for the coin operator. The dynamics are governed by unitary evolution operators.

**Key observables.** Probability amplitudes ($\alpha, eta, \gamma$) and the limiting probability density function $\Psi(t, z, y)$ that solves the Dirac PDEs.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of states (3), the coin matrix $C$ (e.g., $e^{i\lambda g_k}$), and the continuum limit parameter ($\epsilon 	o 0$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on establishing weak convergence using Poisson processes to bridge the gap between discrete quantum evolution and continuous PDE solutions.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare simulation results for various coins (Hadamard, Grover) showing both unitary evolution benchmarks against the derived probabilistic representation in spacetime plots.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from reviewing the two-state case to extending the construction using Gell-Mann matrices for three states. It then rigorously derives the Poisson process formulation and finally establishes the convergence of this discrete walk to a set of coupled Dirac PDEs via rescaling.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Building upon the pioneering framework of Vu (2026), we construct a probabilistic representation for three-state discrete-time quantum walks on integer lattices and validate it through empirical examples. Furthermore, we establish that this representation converges to the continuum solution of multi-state Dirac partial differential equations. Broadly, our findings demonstrate that this probabilistic paradigm serves as a robust alternative for simulating higher-dimensional quantum walks, opening new theoretical avenues to analyze quantum dynamics using classical stochastic processes.

</details>
